Why I’d Pick Economy Over Premium Economy On An Overnight Flight

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1061 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I just got back to Rio after a quick trip to Ireland for Aer Lingus’ event to showcase their fresh A330 cabins, including its first-ever premium economy.
  • Industry observers note that I flew Air France economy both ways, and I’m glad I resisted the offer of $420 during online check-in to upgrade the outbound overnight economy leg.
  • premium economy question, it all comes down to maximising comfort, and I think this is easier to do in economy than premium economy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I just got back to Rio after a quick trip to Ireland for Aer Lingus’ event to showcase their fresh A330 cabins, including its first-ever premium economy.

Industry observers note that I flew Air France economy both ways, and I’m glad I resisted the offer of $420 during online check-in to upgrade the outbound overnight economy leg. Ironically, it was the long day-flight back where I actually wished I’d upgraded.

However, to answer the economy vs. premium economy question, it all comes down to maximising comfort, and I think this is easier to do in economy than premium economy.

If, like me, sleeping upright or on your back is almost impossible, then what follows will likely apply to you.

The main reason I’m deterred to pick premium economy for overnight flights is because of the fixed armrests, where tray tables are sometimes stowed in this cabin.

Despite the extra recline and leg rest element (which sometimes makes it even harder to get comfortable), the fixed armrests restrict the ability to sleep any way other than straight like a pencil.

To make matters worse, they stop you from lying across more than one seat if you find yourself in an empty row.

Recent findings suggest that it’s for that reason that I much prefer economy. While having a row to yourself isn’t guaranteed, there’s at least a chance of being able to move around the cabin, or stretch out into an empty seat. No matter where you sit or how empty the cabin is, you can’t do that in premium economy.

Another element of my pre-trip planning that I expect many of you to relate to is the fact it takes me so long umming and aahing over the best seat to pick.

Thanks to my Flying Blue Gold status (SkyTeam Elite Plus), I could pick any seat in the economy cabin of the Boeing 777-200ER for free from 72 hours before departure.

In a recent development, I narrowed it down to an empty seat in the exit row, and the only row of three with an empty middle seat. I didn’t even consider one of the many empty middle rows of four seats in case they filled up before take off and I ended up in an aisle with no window to rest my head. Using the window or plane’s fuselage to rest my head on is the only saving grace for me when trying to sleep sitting upright.

As the empty exit seat would have the same restricting fixed partition as premium, I decided against that, too.

According to recent reports, after the “boarding complete” announcement was made, the middle seat in my row remained empty, and there were three seats free in the middle of row 25, a row in front. I explained to the girl in the aisle seat that if one of us moved to the other row, we’d both have three seats to ourselves. She didn’t seem to understand my point, and noted she’d prefer to sit in the aisle than us both have three free seats to ourselves.

I didn’t want to move to the middle seats either, so I got as comfortable as I could using the middle seat and the pillow I brought from home.

Recent findings suggest that in the end, I did manage to get some half decent curled up shut eye (the thick pillow protected my back from the hard parts of the seat when propped against the fuselage). However, when I went to the loo, I noticed some people in the rear cabin had got lucky and were fast asleep spread across a whole four seats.

Maybe I’ll take more of a risk next time….

I’m not saying economy is always a better choice than premium. For example, I’d always recommend Emirates’ pretty darn impressive premium economy over economy, because it genuinely is several steps up from economy.

According to recent reports, if it was up to me, I’d have had a lie-flat seat for the overnight segment. I didn’t, and I’m pretty certain I got better sleep quality curled up across two seats in economy that I would have almost upright on my back in premium.

Would you ever choose economy over premium economy?

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, the lame-duck session continues as lawmakers look ahead to Thanksgiving and the funding deadline that arrives in December.
  • Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally launched a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally released a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

According to recent reports, the lame-duck session continues as lawmakers look ahead to Thanksgiving and the funding deadline that arrives in December. The primary legislative business this week is the Senate's bipartisan permitting overhaul, but a late-breaking aviation funding fight and the Senate Democratic leadership contest are also commanding attention.

Sources indicate that sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally launched a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., and both men are accumulating supporters ahead of leadership votes that are currently scheduled for early December — though there's been an effort to move that up to this week.

Van Hollen has expressed disagreement with Schumer's participation in primaries.

​"I don't think it's the role of the Senate majority leader to get involved in open, contested Democratic primaries," Van Hollen mentioned Sunday on CNN.

In a recent development, ​Van Hollen has also noted he wants to use all available tools to stop funding for the Iran war immediately, with a government funding deadline in December. That's going to be one of several flash points for December's funding discussions, as President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans try to use what leverage they have before Democrats take the gavels in the House and the Senate in January.

A new problem is the state of federal air traffic control after Friday's nationwide ground stop, with the Trump administration now seeking $50 billion to upgrade systems.

"I need additional money to do the additional work to keep the airspace safe," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Fox News Sunday.

Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, a senior appropriator who is in line to become majority whip, has suggested reallocating funds from the additional money the Trump administration and congressional Republicans allocated to Immigration and Customs Enforcement to address the challenges at the Federal Aviation Administration.

"There is a pot of 60 billion extra dollars on top of the regularly appropriated amount for ICE and we should use at least a portion of that money for the FAA. We can solve this problem and not spend any additional taxpayer dollars," Schatz posted on X.

Sources indicate that "We can do all things, we don't have to do one versus the other," Duffy noted in the Fox News Sunday interview. "I don't think that is the answer. The answer is let's do everything that's going to keep Americans safe, whether it's with immigration or it's with air travel.".

According to recent reports, meanwhile on the Senate floor, the energy permitting overhaul bill faces a key test Monday evening​, with a vote scheduled to limit debate on a substitute amendment that represents the most recent version of the bill. Votes on a number of President Donald Trump's judicial nominations are also lined up this week.

Sources indicate that on the other side of the Capitol, the House floor schedule i​ncludes several labor-related bills. ​One of the measures, introduced by Sen.-elect Kevin Hern, R-Okla.,​ would set standards for the way labor law applies to franchise operators.

Latest member orientation is also continuing, and committees in both the House and Senate will be holding hearings throughout the week as the outgoing Republican committee chairs aim to get through priority items on their agenda before the end of the Congress.

It has been revealed that that includes a Tuesday morning Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing for Hung Cao, the nominee to be Navy secretary, who is at the moment the acting secretary. The Senate Judiciary Committee will be busy as well, as Chairman Charles E. Grassley, R-Iowa, looks to tee up more of Trump's judicial nominations for floor consideration.

    #88796. Third Time’s Not The Charm: A SWISS A220’s Odd Triple Aborted Takeoff

    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    Third Time’s Not The Charm: A SWISS A220’s Odd Triple Aborted Takeoff

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (987 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that if you’re a frequent flyer, odds are that you’ve encountered an aborted takeoff, whereby the plane accelerates down the runway, only to slow down, and eventually come to a stop.
    • It has been revealed that however, here’s something you don’t often see — a SWISS Airbus A220 aborted its takeoff three times in a row, before finally returning to the gate to see what was going on, as reported by Blick.
    • Sources indicate that on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, SWISS flight LX2110 was scheduled to operate from Zurich (ZRH) to Malaga (AGP), with a 9:35AM departure.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that if you’re a frequent flyer, odds are that you’ve encountered an aborted takeoff, whereby the plane accelerates down the runway, only to slow down, and eventually come to a stop. In some cases this can feel like a non-event, while in other cases it can feel much scarier, depending on the speed at which the takeoff is aborted.

    It has been revealed that however, here’s something you don’t often see — a SWISS Airbus A220 aborted its takeoff three times in a row, before finally returning to the gate to see what was going on, as reported by Blick. The explanation is actually quite logical, but that doesn’t make the whole ordeal any less unusual.

    Sources indicate that on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, SWISS flight LX2110 was scheduled to operate from Zurich (ZRH) to Malaga (AGP), with a 9:35AM departure. The flight was operated by an Airbus A220-300 with the registration code HB-JCM.

    The plane pushed back and taxied out to the runway right on schedule. The pilots began the takeoff roll, but then quickly applied the brakes, causing the plane to come to a stop, while still at a slow speed. The pilots took a moment to run checklists, and then decided on another takeoff attempt, only for the same thing to happen again!

    Recent findings suggest that after the second aborted takeoff, the captain reportedly informed passengers that the thrust levers had popped out during the takeoff roll, and that was the reason for the aborted takeoff. However, rather than returning to the gate, they decided to attempt an additional takeoff roll.

    Once again, the takeoff was aborted. At that point the captain explained that nothing like this had ever happened to him before in his 12 year career, and that the plane would be returning to the gate.

    There ended up being a plane change, and then the A220 with the registration code HB-JCO was assigned to operate this flight — it ended up taking off at 1:29PM and landing at 3:52PM, around 3.5 hours behind schedule.

    A SWISS spokesperson confirmed the incident happened, though noted that the takeoffs were aborted at a low speed of around 50 kilometers per hour (around 30 miles per hour).

    Sources indicate that what explains the aborted takeoffs? Well, it was because as the plane accelerated for takeoff, the automatic thrust control system automatically deactivated. To explain this as simply as possible, as I understand it, on the A220 when the auto-thrust is armed and the thrust levers are moved forward for takeoff, the auto-thrust then takes over, and moves the levers forward without manual intervention.

    Industry observers note that in other words, one of the pilots keeps their hands on the auto-thrust levers and “moves” with them, but doesn’t actually apply any force. Pilots are trained this way, and to not manually apply force. In the event that the crew tries to stop the auto-thrust lever motion, a pressure switch detects this, and then disengages the auto-thrust, to allow for a manual override.

    It has been revealed that in this case, the auto-thrust incorrectly detected resistance, when the pilots weren’t attempting to apply it. According to the airline, the system that monitors the aircraft’s technical status in real time was unable to identify the cause of the error, as no errors were displayed in the system. So at first, the pilots likely wondered if they had accidentally applied force.

    However, once technicians had a look at the plane, it was discovered that the switch for disabling the automatic thrust control on the original aircraft was stuck, and this caused the automatic thrust control to shut down during takeoff attempts.

    So while this can understandably seem scary to passengers, this wasn’t even a direct safety issue. After all, the pilots could’ve also manually moved the throttles. However, you also don’t want to take off when you know there’s an issue with the throttles, since that’s not exactly a best practice.

    Industry observers note that A SWISS Airbus A220 attempted a takeoff from Zurich three times in a row. While I’ve had two consecutive aborted takeoffs, I’ve never had three, and I can’t imagine that happens all too often.

    While this is unusual, it sounds like this was handled well, and I can see why the pilots kept trying. This wasn’t a critical safety issue, but instead, just an incorrect detection of inputs, in a way that wouldn’t really pose a risk to the flight. At the same time, you don’t want to knowingly take off with a fault switch.

    What do you make of this SWISS aborted takeoff trio?

    #88795. The Airlines Set To Replace Their Boeing 777s With New 777-9s Throughout The 2030s

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1708 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    The Airlines Set To Replace Their Boeing 777s With New 777-9s Throughout The 2030s

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1708 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Boeing has roughly 620 orders for an aircraft that has not delivered a single one yet, and some of the very first examples built may never reach the airline that paid for them.
    • So who is really lining up to replace their Boeing 777s with the fresh 777-9, what exactly are they replacing, and when will passengers see the first one?
    • The scale of the commitment is hard to ignore.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Boeing has roughly 620 orders for an aircraft that has not delivered a single one yet, and some of the very first examples built may never reach the airline that paid for them. The 777-9 is meant to be the jet that carries the world's biggest long-haul airlines through the 2030s, but the program is about seven years behind its original 2020 service date, and the biggest customer has already turned away its first batch. For an industry that intends fleets decades ahead, that is a very awkward way to start a fresh era.

    So who is really lining up to replace their Boeing 777s with the fresh 777-9, what exactly are they replacing, and when will passengers see the first one? The answers involve Emirates, Qatar Airways, Cathay Pacific, Singapore Airlines, and Lufthansa, plus a rival Airbus that has already started delivering.

    The scale of the commitment is hard to ignore. According to an order book compiled by Airways Magazine at the end of May 2026, the 777X program stood at 619 orders: 521 777-9s, 63 777-8 freighters, and 35 passenger 777-8s, all of them for Emirates. That is a remarkable number for an aircraft that has not carried a single paying passenger, and it makes the 777X Boeing's most crucial widebody bet of the decade. Airways also noted that the problem is certification, not demand, which is a rare thing to say about a program this delayed.

    Emirates dominates the list. As reported by Emirates itself, its November 2025 Dubai Airshow deal added 65 more 777-9s, worth $38 billion at list prices, and lifted its total to 270 777Xs. The airline also holds options to convert part of that order into the 777-8 or the proposed, larger 777-10. Airways lists the split as 235 777-9s and 35 777-8s, so the exact mix is still fluid. Qatar Airways is second with 124 aircraft, made up of 90 777-9s and 34 777-8 freighters, followed by Cathay Pacific with 35 and Singapore Airlines with 31.

    Recent findings suggest that british Airways and its parent IAG have 24, Lufthansa Group has 27 (20 passenger jets and seven freighters), Korean Air has 20, and ANA has 20, including two freighters. Air India, Etihad, and Ethiopian Airlines hold 10, 10, and 8. But a long list of customers only tells us who wants the jet. It says nothing about what each of them intends to retire in exchange, or how long they will have to keep the old aircraft flying while they wait.

    In a recent development, for most buyers, the answer is the Boeing 777-300ER, the best-selling long-haul widebody of its generation. Emirates alone flies 119 of them, plus 10 777-200LRs, according to its own fleet table. As noted by Simple Flying, the 777X is also pitched as a successor to high-capacity four-engine jets such as the Boeing 747 and the Airbus A380, which burn far more fuel and cost more to maintain.

    In a recent development, the new jet's biggest selling point is efficiency. According to Simple Flying's analysis of range and capacity, the 777-9 seats around 426 passengers against roughly 396 on a 777-300ER, while keeping a nearly identical range. The GE9X engines are expected to deliver up to 10% better fuel efficiency than the GE90-115B engines on the older jet.

    The wing is the other trick: it spans 235 feet, 5 inches (71.8 meters) in flight, but its tips fold to 212 feet, 9 inches (64.9 meters) on the ground so it still fits standard gates. Boeing's pitch to airlines is simple: keep the long range, burn less fuel, and spend less on maintenance than the aging jets on the ramp.

    Boeing 777-300ER vs. 777-9: the swap in numbers.

    7,370 nautical miles (13,649 km).

    7,285 nautical miles (13,492 km).

    242 feet, 4 inches (73.9 meters).

    251 feet, 9 inches (76.7 meters).

    GE9X (up to 10% better efficiency).

    Recent findings suggest that on paper, that is a clean trade: more seats, similar range, lower fuel burn. The uncomfortable detail is that the older jets have to keep flying while the replacement is late, and that raises a very practical question about timing. Airways Magazine points out that carriers waiting on the 777-9 have had to stretch the lives of older 777-300ERs, A380s, and 747-400s, which adds maintenance, fuel, and cabin-product pressure with every extra year.

    Recent findings suggest that lufthansa will be the first, with Boeing targeting a 2027 delivery. Emirates mentioned in November 2025 that it expects its first 777-9 from the second quarter of 2027, and its Boeing deliveries stretch all the way to 2038. That means the airline will be swapping 777-300ERs for 777-9s for more than a decade, which is exactly why this story belongs to the 2030s rather than to next year. Emirates still flies 116 Airbus A380s as well, so the transition will be gradual rather than a clean break.

    Sources indicate that others will wait longer. According to Simple Flying, citing the Mainly Miles blog, Singapore Airlines' fleet plan indicates no 777-9 deliveries in the 12 months to March 31, 2027, with Emirates, Qatar Airways, and Lufthansa ahead in the queue. That timing matters because Singapore Airlines is also planning a latest premium economy product around the aircraft, making the 777-9 part of a future cabin strategy as well as a fleet replacement program.

    According to recent reports, even the schedule itself is soft. Airways Magazine reported that FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford signaled the 777X would follow the 737 MAX 7 and MAX 10 into 2027 for certification. So queue position is one thing, but the airlines cannot simply take delivery because they are next in line. The more awkward problem is already sitting on Boeing's property: aircraft built years ago for customers that may no longer want them.

    Sources indicate that between 2019 and 2021, Boeing built around 30 777-9s before the program stalled, including aircraft earmarked for Emirates and Lufthansa, according to German aviation outlet aero.de. By the time they could be delivered, they would be about eight years old and technically behind the final production standard. That creates an unusual problem for a brand-latest aircraft: the earliest examples are already old enough to require substantial work before an airline wants them.

    As reported by Simple Flying, Emirates rejected the first batch built for it because bringing those airframes up to the required standard would take extensive and costly rework. Boeing reportedly dismantled one early Emirates-bound 777-9 after the cost to fix it exceeded its value. Lufthansa has since noted, on its second-quarter earnings call, that it will refuse some of its earliest aircraft, with Boeing contributing financially to upgrade the rest.

    Qatar Airways has reportedly signaled that it does not want early-build aircraft either, so Boeing may pool the rejected jets and sell them in bundles. According to aero.de, an unnamed US airline is reportedly interested in 20 early 777-9s, which is striking because no major US carrier has ordered the type at all. A discounted early-build 777-9 could therefore find a newly introduced home, but the fact that airlines that ordered the aircraft in the first place are turning some away highlights just how unusual this delay has become.

    Recent findings suggest that according to Simple Flying, Qatar Airways put the A350-1000 into service in February 2018, the 777-9 first flew in January 2020 and still was not certified at Farnborough 2026, and Airbus has already delivered 114 A350-1000s against 367 firm orders. Boeing, meanwhile, has delivered none of its more than 520 777-9s.

    Industry observers note that air Canada is the clearest example. As reported by Business Traveller, the airline ordered eight A350-1000s, with options on eight more, for delivery from the second half of 2030, to modernize a long-haul fleet that includes 19 777-300ERs. Business Traveller calls the A350-1000 a logical replacement for the 777-300ER, and notes it brings a cabin altitude of about 6,000 feet (1,829 meters) versus 8,000 feet (2,438 meters) on the 777 family. No North American airline has ordered the 777-9, so for passengers in the US and Canada, the A350-1000 may arrive first.

    Still, a head start is not the same as a better fit. The 777-9 carries more passengers, and for airlines that fill every seat, that may be the decisive metric. The A350-1000 offers the established nine-abreast cabin and a substantial operating track record, while Boeing's aircraft offers greater capacity and is aimed squarely at airlines that need to move huge numbers of passengers through constrained hubs. That leaves the 777-9 with a clear market, but a narrower one than the raw order total might suggest.

    The honest answer is volume and density. Emirates and Qatar Airways run some of the busiest trunk routes in the world, and for those carriers, the 777-9's size is a feature rather than a flaw. An A350-1000 cannot match its seat count, and the A380 is out of production, so the 777-9 is effectively the last big twin-engine option left for airlines that need capacity above all else. That is the strongest argument Boeing has, and it is also why the aircraft is best suited to a relatively small group of mega-hub operators.

    The test comes in the next 18 months. If Lufthansa takes its first jet in 2027 and Emirates follows soon after, the long order book will start to look like a steady delivery stream. If certification slips again, as Airways Magazine warns could compress the entire handover and training timeline, more carriers may do what Air Canada did and look at the A350-1000 instead. The early-build jets will be worth watching too: how many Boeing can remarket, and at what price, will reveal just how costly the delay has been.

    In a recent development, emirates has even signed options to stretch part of its order into the 777-10, a bigger variant Boeing is still studying. That may ultimately be the most revealing sign of all: the airlines that have waited longest for the 777-9 are still thinking about what comes after it. By 2035, the question may no longer be whether the 777-9 replaced the 777-300ER. It may be whether Boeing's biggest twinjet has finally found the narrow but extremely valuable market it was designed for.

    Biden: ‘Hard to take’ as Pelosi, Schumer turned on him in 2024

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that president Joe Biden, Speaker Nancy Pelosi, and Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., arrive for The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 bill signing at the White House, on Aug.
    • In a recent development, in conversations with Democratic strategists in recent months, I heard a strikingly similar sentiment when the topic turned to Joe Biden’s forthcoming memoir.
    • Spoiler alert: Biden offers only a full-throated defense of his decision to seek reelection in 2024, and expresses deep disappointment over what he casts as a disloyal pressure campaign orchestrated by party leaders to force him out of the presidential race despite what he cites as his successes in the office.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that president Joe Biden, Speaker Nancy Pelosi, and Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., arrive for The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 bill signing at the White House, on Aug. 9, 2022. In his newly introduced memoir, Biden noted he was disappointed when Pelosi and Schumer urged him to drop out of the presidential race in 2024. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    In a recent development, in conversations with Democratic strategists in recent months, I heard a strikingly similar sentiment when the topic turned to Joe Biden’s forthcoming memoir. The consensus view, even among some who’d worked for the former president, was that if he did anything other than accept some responsibility for his role in Donald Trump’s return to the White House, they didn’t have much appetite to hear what he had to say about anything else.

    Spoiler alert: Biden offers only a full-throated defense of his decision to seek reelection in 2024, and expresses deep disappointment over what he casts as a disloyal pressure campaign orchestrated by party leaders to force him out of the presidential race despite what he cites as his successes in the office.

    But while his perspective on the climactic moment of his political career will be the most scrutinized portion of Biden’s latest book, “Promise Me, America” seems primarily intended to offer the former president a platform he has otherwise not had since leaving office: to catalog what he sees as his historic achievements and offer his perspective on how he wrestled with the major complications of our time.

    It’s often mentioned that the only thing better than being president is being a former president. That has hardly been the case for Biden in the nearly 22 months since he left the White House, especially as he’s endured what his son Hunter has described as “debilitating” physical pain following a cancer diagnosis last March.

    But where “Thanks, Obama” became a popular mantra nearly a decade ago for Democrats seeking to defend and celebrate the 44th president’s record in contrast with the first Trump administration, no such widespread nostalgia has emerged around Biden, as the party is loath to revisit the trauma of the summer of 2024.

    The sheer length of his new book — more than 400 pages — seems an implicit acknowledgment that presenting a positive portrait of Biden’s single term in office is largely to be a solitary effort. Over 15 chapters, Biden offers sometimes mechanical descriptions of specific policies and their impact, but also new details of the sausage-making required to pass major initiatives like the Inflation Reduction Act. That legislation, he writes, was revived thanks in part to an Italian dinner hosted by Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo to make peace between West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin III and White House Chief of Staff Ron Klain.

    Biden writes in sweeping terms about other accomplishments like responding to the COVID-19 crisis he inherited, calling his administration’s work “one of the most monumental achievements in public health history.” He repeatedly defends his frequent efforts to warn Americans about the need to safeguard our democracy even as critics in the press and his own party suggested he focus more on economic concerns.

    Industry observers note that supporting Ukraine in its war against Russia gets the most extensive treatment of any single glitch in the book, including a detailed account of Biden’s clandestine trip to Kyiv in February 2023. And the former Senate Foreign Relations Committee chairman takes great effort to delve into the complexity of the U.S.-China relationship and his relationship with President Xi Jinping, while asserting that Taiwan “will likely be the most important foreign policy challenge in the world over the next generation.”.

    Recent findings suggest that recurring throughout the book are expressions of optimism that under his administration, Washington was beginning to work again like it was supposed to, that America’s global leadership was being restored through its alliances, and that he was tackling problems that previous presidents had sidestepped. And in offering this comprehensive presentation of his record, Biden also offers his primary rationale for running again.

    Industry observers note that “We had accomplished so much —  I wanted to finish the job. And yes: I believed I was the best person to do it,” he says. “I was the only person who had ever beaten Donald Trump. And I felt I was the best person to do it again.”.

    One of Biden’s top advisers put it to me a different way in the months leading up to his decision to seek another term. “He has been running for president for 50 years. And the idea that he would actually be president and stop running for president is almost laughably preposterous.”.

    The biggest question, of course, was his age, something Biden, who was 81 when he dropped out of the race, asserts he gave serious consideration.

    Sources indicate that “I knew better than anyone how old I was. I knew what I was —  and wasn’t —  capable of doing. I carefully monitored how I was meeting the demands of the job. And there is not a single example of me failing to handle my responsibilities,” he writes.

    The June 27 debate, of course, created a very different perception, as Biden acknowledges that his flubbed comment that “we finally beat Medicare” was to become “Exhibit A that I was too old to do the job.” But he tries to argue it was no different than the poor showings of previous incumbent presidents, including President Barack Obama, in their first debates.

    According to recent reports, “The difference was that every other president was given the chance to redeem themselves in a second debate. As it turned out, that chance would not be available to me,” Biden writes.

    He argues the response he was seeing from voters at his public events after the debate didn’t justify the panicked response of elected Democrats in Washington, and that public polling showed only minor slippage after the debate, until a steady drumbeat of elected Democrats publicly began calling for him to step aside.

    Describing separate visits from former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., personally urging him to step aside, he claims there was a “yawning gap between what I was seeing with Democratic voters and what I was hearing from the Democratic leadership in Washington.”.

    “I have to admit it was personally hard to take so many old friends turning on me,” Biden claims. “I told Schumer he had a lot of gumption (I may have said it differently at the time), coming to my home and telling me to get out of the race. Loyalty matters to me. If I give you my word, I stick with you. If I say I’m with you, I’m with you to the end.”.

    At one point, Biden seems to reflect some resentment that some of the Democrats who would ultimately call on him to drop out of the race had themselves been too afraid to challenge him in the first place, saying: “Anyone who was scared off from running has no business being president.” While there was a constant narrative about the weakness of his candidacy, Biden acknowledges, the lack of a serious challenger was in fact a sign of his strength.

    It has been revealed that “I had it on good authority that several massive names in Democratic politics had looked at running. They held meetings and took polls and talked to donors and to potential staff. If they thought I was weak or vulnerable, they would have taken their shot. But they didn’t,” he writes.

    According to recent reports, biden’s defiant tone, and his insistence that the lack of party unity was a greater threat to his continued candidacy than his own performance, may be dismissed by Democrats who don’t want to revisit this difficult chapter. But as Schumer and other Democratic leaders are now facing their own internal challenges, “Promise Me, America” may also serve as a cautionary note for an ambitious crop of potential candidates hoping to reclaim the presidency in 2028.

    I’ve gotta say, huge kudos to Mexico’s President, Claudia Sheinbaum, for setting quite the example in terms of how she recently traveled to China, as flagged by View from the Wing….

    World leaders have just met in Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders’ Meeting. As you’d expect, most leaders flew on their government planes. There were some exceptions, though I can’t imagine anyone else flew the same way as Mexico’s 64-year-old president.

    Viajamos hacia Shenzhen para representar a México en el Foro de Cooperación Económica Asia-Pacífico (APEC) China 2026; la agenda de actividades incluye reunión con empresarios de países miembros. Además, participaré en la conferencia de prensa matutina para informar avances de… pic.twitter.com/F9UqRLjFlb.

    Media reports suggest she flew to China on China Southern. Specifically, she traveled on Sunday, November 15, 2026, on CZ8032, from Mexico City (MEX) to Shenzhen (SZX), with a refueling stop in Tijuana (TIJ), and the journey covering a distance of 8,803 miles.

    In a recent development, the Airbus A350-900 took off from Mexico City at 12:49AM, arriving in Tijuana at 2:02AM, after a flight time of 3hr13min. Then it took off again at 4:34AM, and landed in Shenzhen the following morning at 11:31AM, after a flight time of 14hr56min. All-in-all, the flight took around 21 hours, including the refueling stop.

    Industry observers note that the shocking thing here isn’t that she traveled commercial, but instead, that she reportedly flew in economy! Reports suggest she was in seat 33B, which would be a middle seat in economy, no less!

    Llegamos a la Ciudad de México en el vuelo CZ8031 desde Shenzhen, China. Agradecemos a toda la tripulación por su apoyo. pic.twitter.com/DSC83CpnDQ.

    I think a head of state should reasonably be able to fly business class on a flight of this length, for two reasons:.

It’s certainly quite a contrast to what we’ve seen here, where President Trump accepted a Boeing 747-8 as a gift from Qatar, and talked about how he has done it to make Americans be proud, because “our country has to be represented properly.” Heck, just this week he talked about “China was very impressed” and “Russia was very impressed” of his latest plane. Lovely, I’m happy we’re impressing Putin, that makes me proud to be an American!

    "Russia was very impressed" — Trump leads his press conference by bragging about taking the longest flight in Air Force One history, in case you were worried that he actually accomplished something useful on his trip pic.twitter.com/dDIHg8wb1w.

    Sources indicate that keep in mind that Mexico has an interesting history when it comes to how leaders fly. In 2016, Mexico’s government took control of a private Boeing 787, which flew around former President Enrique Pena Nieto. The purchase of the plane had actually been arranged under the previous president, Felipe Calderón, in 2012.

    It has been revealed that then in 2018, when Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador took charge in Mexico, he fulfilled a campaign promise of selling that 787, which turned out to be pretty challenging, given that demand for a secondhand VIP 787 isn’t exactly that high (the plane ended up going to Tajikistan). Sheinbaum has kept that general legacy going, by flying commercial.

    Mexico’s President, Claudia Sheinbaum, traveled to the recent summit in China differently than virtually all other government leaders. Not only did she fly commercial, but she traveled in economy, and reportedly even in a middle seat.

    Industry observers note that there’s no denying that this is more about optics than anything, but I very much respect that. It’s nice to see heads of state who lead by example, as it’s pretty rare to see nowadays.

    #88792. Why JSX Just Bought Upcoming Pacific Airlines, The Strange, Failed 757 Startup

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1019 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    Why JSX Just Bought Upcoming Pacific Airlines, The Strange, Failed 757 Startup

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1019 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Public charter air carrier JSX has just acquired Fresh Pacific Airlines, and with this, New Pacific Airlines intends to resume flights, with Embraer E145 aircraft.
    • If you’re not familiar with New Pacific Airlines, you’re probably thinking “huh?” If you are familiar with New Pacific Airlines, you’re probably thinking “WTF?” There’s a sneaky and logical explanation here, so let me explain.
    • Sources indicate that let’s start with a little context.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Public charter air carrier JSX has just acquired Fresh Pacific Airlines, and with this, New Pacific Airlines intends to resume flights, with Embraer E145 aircraft.

    If you’re not familiar with New Pacific Airlines, you’re probably thinking “huh?” If you are familiar with New Pacific Airlines, you’re probably thinking “WTF?” There’s a sneaky and logical explanation here, so let me explain.

    Sources indicate that let’s start with a little context. JSX is a public charter air carrier, which operates a fleet of nearly 60 planes, most of which are Embraer E135s and E145s.

    It operates as a Part 135 operator, meaning it’s not technically an airline, as it’s using a loophole that allows it to not use standard TSA security screening, hire pilots with fewer than 1,500 hours, etc. Basically what’s happening is that one subsidiary sells the tickets, and then another subsidiary operates the flights, so it’s technically a “charter” (with 30 people who don’t know one another).

    Then there’s Upcoming Pacific Airlines, one of the strangest airline startups we’ve ever seen, and which I’ve covered extensively. The airline acquired some Boeing 757s, and the business strategy was to connect North America and Asia via Anchorage (ANC).

    Industry observers note that the business model made zero sense in the first place, though there was some funding there, and they even invested in constructing a lounge in Anchorage, even though those flights never did happen. The airline did briefly fly from (ONT) to Nashville (BNA) — as one does — before ultimately going out of business.

    That brings us to the news. Upcoming Pacific Airlines intends to resume flights with Embraer E145s that are leased from JSX, as reported by IshrionA. According to a Department of Transportation filing, the airline intends to resume flights with planes featuring 42 seats, which is higher than the 30-seat limit you’ll find on current JSX planes.

    Sources indicate that JSX acquires Latest Pacific Airlines.New Pacific Airlines intends to resume flights with ERJ 145 leased from JSX. pic.twitter.com/uMMS0J2fZy.

    In a recent development, on the surface, this of course makes absolutely no sense. Latest Pacific Airlines was out of business, and the business model made no sense. So why would JSX buy an airline and then lease planes to it?

    Industry observers note that long story short, this seems to be a play to acquire a cheap Part 121 certificate. A Part 121 operator is a firm that’s allowed to operate scheduled air transport… in other words, a “real” airline. As I mentioned above, JSX has historically been a Part 135 operator, and that explicitly means it’s not an airline. It’s a public charter air carrier, so it’s not a “real” airline.

    In a recent development, going back a couple of years, we know that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) was considering cracking down on carriers like JSX, since they definitely don’t operate within the spirit of the rules. That’s not to say that JSX did anything wrong, because by the letter of the law, they’re following it exactly. It’s just that the letter of the law makes no sense, and clearly doesn’t reflect the intent behind distinguishing between Part 121 and Part 135 operators.

    According to recent reports, under Trump, there was no scrutiny of this. However, with Democrats soon controlling both the House and Senate, I imagine JSX leaders may be worried that there could again be more scrutiny. If nothing else, buying a cheap Part 121 certificate is a good insurance policy, in case the government does crack down. After all, these can basically be “sold,” while acquiring one from scratch can be grueling process.

    I wouldn’t assume that anything will really operate with Fresh Pacific Airlines branding, or based on a New Pacific Airlines business model. Instead, I imagine the idea is that JSX will start dabbling in Part 121 operations, which is why these planes will have more seats (above the 30-seat cap that’s allowed), since that’s no longer a factor.

    Sources indicate that if the government were to crack down on Part 135 operators, JSX could move to Part 121 operations. However, they’d have to make lots of changes, from their pilot hiring, to the way passengers are screened.

    JSX has just bought Upcoming Pacific, the airline with an absurd business model that went bankrupt. No, JSX isn’t inspired by the concept of flying Boeing 757s to Asia. Instead, this is clearly the cheapest way for JSX to acquire a Part 121 certificate, which would be required for the carrier to continue operations in the event that the government were to crack down on the Part 135 operator loophole.

    It’s going to be interesting to see how this evolves, both since JSX seems to have aims to operate Part 121 operations in the near future, and also to see how JSX’s business model would evolve if the Part 135 concept were blocked.

    What do you make of this JSX Part 121 play?

    Why Airliners Cruise Around 35,000 Feet Instead Of Flying Lower Or Higher

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1869 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, if you glance at the flight map on the seatback screen, the number indicating the aircraft altitude is almost always the same: 35,000 feet (10,668 meters).
    • The thin air that makes high-altitude flying cheaper also takes lift away from the wings and thrust away from the engines, while the safety margin narrows with every thousand feet.
    • Recent findings suggest that that compromise starts with something passengers rarely notice from the cabin: there is dramatically less atmosphere at 35,000 feet than there is at sea level.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, if you glance at the flight map on the seatback screen, the number indicating the aircraft altitude is almost always the same: 35,000 feet (10,668 meters). No law demands it, and no airline manual treats it as sacred. But jet airliners flying from Seattle to Singapore keep settling into the same narrowband of sky, as if the atmosphere came with a built-in parking spot.

    The thin air that makes high-altitude flying cheaper also takes lift away from the wings and thrust away from the engines, while the safety margin narrows with every thousand feet. The result is a constant compromise between aerodynamics, engine performance, aircraft weight, winds, and air traffic control. And the altitude that makes the most sense at the beginning of a long flight may be completely different several hours later.

    Recent findings suggest that that compromise starts with something passengers rarely notice from the cabin: there is dramatically less atmosphere at 35,000 feet than there is at sea level. According to AirportFYI, the International Standard Atmosphere puts air at about 31% of its sea-level density at 35,000 feet, or roughly 0.024 pounds per cubic foot (0.38 kg per cubic meter). Just imagine wading through a swimming pool versus walking through an ankle-deep puddle. Less air means less drag, and drag is one of the biggest fuel penalties an aircraft has to overcome. If you prefer to see the idea rather than read it, this YouTube explainer tackles the same question visually.

    Industry observers note that that reduction in density is one reason modern airliners spend so much of their cruise above most weather systems. The cabin, of course, cannot simply follow the outside atmosphere. At 35,000 feet, the air outside is far too thin to breathe normally, which is why pressurized cabins are maintained at an equivalent altitude of roughly 6,000 to 8,000 feet (1,800 to 2,400 meters). Temperature helps the equation as well. The standard atmosphere at 35,000 feet is around minus 66°F (minus 54°C), and the speed of sound falls to about 660 mph (1,062 km/h), compared with 761 mph (1,225 km/h) at sea level. AirportFYI notes that modern swept-wing jets typically cruise between Mach 0.78 and 0.85 there, roughly 515 to 560 mph (830 to 900 km/h). As reported by Military & Aerospace Electronics, thinner air reduces drag and lets an aircraft cover more distance for the fuel it burns.

    Industry observers note that that is the attraction of altitude. But reducing the air around an aircraft also reduces the air available to its wings and engines. Eventually, climbing higher stops being an efficiency trick and becomes a performance problem.

    It has been revealed that the same thin air that makes cruise economical creates the next limitation. A wing still has to produce enough lift to support the aircraft, and lift depends partly on air density and the square of airspeed. At roughly 31% of sea-level density, an airliner has to fly substantially faster through the air, or operate at a higher angle of attack, to generate the lift required to carry the same weight. Military & Aerospace Electronics explains that an aircraft can compensate through speed and angle of attack, but it cannot keep climbing indefinitely and expect performance to remain unchanged.

    Engines face their own problem. As Your Mileage May Vary points out, there are fewer oxygen molecules available for combustion at high altitude, reducing engine thrust. The climb itself also costs fuel, so gaining altitude is only worthwhile when the efficiency gained during cruise outweighs the energy spent getting there. NASA describes cruise efficiency as a function of the aircraft, its engines, and its operating conditions rather than a single ideal altitude.

    The table also explains why flying lower is not the answer. At 10,000 feet (3,048 meters), a jet encounters more than twice the air density it does at 35,000 feet, meaning considerably more aerodynamic resistance. It is also closer to weather and other traffic. Yet the best altitude is not fixed, because the aircraft itself changes throughout the flight.

    In a recent development, A long-haul aircraft leaves the gate carrying tons of fuel and gradually gets lighter as that fuel is burned. That changes the altitude at which it can operate most efficiently. Military & Aerospace Electronics explains that an aircraft's weight can make a higher altitude less efficient early in a flight or leave too little performance margin to climb there. NASA likewise describes optimum cruise altitude as closely tied to aircraft weight.

    AirportFYI offers an illustrative example: a heavily loaded Boeing 777-300ER flying from Dubai to London might begin with an optimum altitude around FL310, or 31,000 feet (9,449 meters), before moving toward FL390, or 39,000 feet (11,887 meters), several hours later. The aircraft does not normally climb continuously. Instead, crews can make staged increases known as step climbs. AirportFYI states these steps are usually 2,000 or 4,000 feet (610 or 1,219 meters), and cites industry studies estimating that optimized step climbs on 12- to 16-hour flights can save 1% to 3% of total fuel compared with remaining at one fixed altitude.

    The gradual climb reflects the aircraft's changing weight: as fuel is burned, the jet becomes lighter and can climb more efficiently. But even a progressively lighter jet eventually reaches a point where going higher brings a new problem: the two boundaries of safe high-altitude flight begin moving toward one another.

    The higher an aircraft climbs, the less room it has between two very different aerodynamic problems. The first is flying too slowly and approaching a stall. The second is flying too quickly and encountering compressibility effects as the airflow over the wing approaches critical Mach. Because the speed of sound falls as temperature drops while the true airspeed required to generate lift rises in thinner air, the two boundaries eventually begin to converge.

    SKYbrary defines the coffin corner as the region where the stall boundary meets the critical Mach boundary, and notes that commercial aircraft generally avoid operating close to it. The Lockheed U-2 provides a much more dramatic illustration. As reported by Migflug, at 70,000 feet (21,336 meters), the spy plane can have as little as five to six knots of margin between its stall speed and the high-speed Mach buffet limit. Most commercial jets are deliberately kept well away from such conditions, and Simple Flying has examined what worries pilots when flying above 40,000 feet, where aerodynamic margins, engine performance and operational limitations become even more relevant.

    Airliners maintain a significant margin from the edge. Airways Magazine reports that certification standards require a maneuvering cushion of at least 0.3 g at the highest operating altitude. According to AirportFYI, the practical ceiling for efficient sustained cruise on modern widebodies is about 41,000 to 43,000 feet (12,497 to 13,106 meters), with aircraft such as the Airbus A350 and Boeing 787 capable of operating somewhat higher than many older designs.

    Recent findings suggest that supersonic aircraft solved the problem differently: Simple Flying has examined how high Concorde flew, with the aircraft routinely operating between roughly 50,000 and 60,000 feet (15,240 to 18,288 meters). A conventional subsonic airliner is designed around a very different compromise. And even after the aircraft has found an altitude that works aerodynamically, the crew does not necessarily get to use it.

    According to recent reports, the optimum altitude calculated for an aircraft is only one piece of the flight plan. Dispatchers and flight crews have to account for the aircraft's weight, fuel burn, winds, weather, and the structure of the airspace before the aircraft ever settles into cruise. Per Your Mileage May Vary, pilots work with airline dispatchers to calculate an ideal altitude based on the aircraft's weight and fuel state, then request that level from air traffic control.

    Winds can overturn the calculation again. A higher altitude might offer less drag but place the aircraft in a stronger headwind, wiping out some or all of the fuel benefit. NASA research has found that the optimum depends partly on weight and the wind profile. AirportFYI puts jet stream cores at roughly 140 to 290 mph (220 to 460 km/h) and cites United Airlines research indicating that wind-optimized routing saved about 1.5% of fuel, or around 660 pounds (300 kg), per transatlantic 777 flight. Controllers also have to separate aircraft, so a crew may be held at a different level because its preferred altitude is occupied. Simple Flying has also looked at why private jets can routinely fly higher than commercial airliners, highlighting how different aircraft and operating requirements can change the altitude equation.

    There is also a deceptively simple reason why an aircraft cannot always choose any altitude it wants: flight levels are organized.

    In US airspace, according to the FAA Aeronautical Information Manual, flights on magnetic courses from 000 to 179 degrees use odd flight levels, while those from 180 to 359 degrees use even ones. Reduced Vertical Separation Minimum, or RVSM, keeps properly equipped aircraft 1,000 feet (305 meters) apart between FL290 and FL410. Controllers assign those levels under the FAA air traffic control rules. So FL350 is not a pre-stabilized altitude. Depending on the aircraft's direction and the airspace involved, another aircraft may be assigned FL340 or FL360. Over the North Atlantic, as reported by Simple Flying, aircraft typically operate between 29,000 and 41,000 feet (8,839 and 12,497 meters) within tightly coordinated routes and procedures.

    That makes the familiar 35,000-foot number look less mysterious. It sits inside a carefully managed system where aircraft performance, direction, traffic, winds, and fuel economy all meet. But the next generation of aircraft could still change where that compromise sits.

    According to recent reports, pushing the cruise ceiling upward is possible, but it requires more than giving an airliner more engine thrust. The wing, engines, structure, pressurization system, and control laws all have to work together in an environment where the aerodynamic margin is already narrowing. Concorde demonstrated that passenger aircraft could routinely operate far above today's conventional cruise levels, but its altitude came with penalties in fuel consumption, noise, complexity and operating cost.

    In a recent development, there is also a less glamorous limit to high-altitude efficiency: the aircraft has to be allowed to use the altitude its designers optimized. AirportFYI cites Eurocontrol studies estimating that European flights burn about 5% more fuel than they would with unconstrained optimal altitudes, largely because traffic prevents crews from using their preferred levels. Programs such as Single European Sky ATM Research (SESAR) and the FAA's NextGen are intended to improve aircraft's ability to follow more efficient trajectories. SESAR has evolved from a long-running ATM research program into the EU's principal mechanism for developing and coordinating the digital technologies needed to modernize Europe's fragmented air traffic management system, with its next major deployment phase now being prepared for 2028.

    Industry observers note that the future of efficient cruise may require the aviation system to better provide each aircraft with the altitude it already needs. When a long-haul flight climbs from FL340 to FL360 several hours after departure, the aircraft is lighter than it was at takeoff, its optimum has moved, and the crew is taking advantage of the fresh balance between lift, drag, engine performance, and fuel burn.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, citi Shop takes some of the work out of saving money online.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, citi Shop takes some of the work out of saving money online. Once you've installed its browser extension, it acts as a shopping portal and coupon hunter all-in-one, rewarding you with statement credits.

    Industry observers note that it has broad reach, too, with more than 5,000 participating online merchants. That's easier than a traditional online shopping portal, which requires you to remember to start at the portal and click through before filling your cart.

    Its ease of use makes it a great resource, but other portals or special discounts may save you more.

    Here's how Citi Shop works and what to consider to determine if it's the best savings path for you.

    According to recent reports, citi Shop is a free browser extension for primary cardholders with an eligible Citi credit card, including ThankYou points cards and cobranded cards. Citi retail and commercial cards are usually ineligible.

    Offers come as either a percentage back or a fixed amount back, and your earnings are applied as a statement credit on the Citi card you selected during enrollment.

    Citi Shop is separate from Citi Merchant Offers, which requires you to enroll in targeted offers with a specific Citi card and then use that card for the qualifying purchase.

    Both Citi Shop and traditional portals give you an extra reward for making purchases they track.

    Sources indicate that but Citi Shop brings potential rebates to you, rather than requiring you to initiate your savings search. The extension automatically displays a pop-up with an available offer when you visit a participating website. You'll have the option to activate the offer before checkout.

    All of Citi Shop's rebates are provided as statement credits, unlike the potential airline miles, hotel points or credit card rewards of traditional portals.

    According to recent reports, what I like about Citi Shop is that it also acts like a shopping assistant. Instead of opening six coupon sites only to discover that every code expired last Tuesday, it handles the scavenger hunt for you and tests available promo codes on your behalf.

    Recent findings suggest that like Capital One Shopping, Citi Shop uses a browser extension. However, Capital One Shopping doesn't require a Capital One card to enroll and its rewards can be redeemed for eligible gift cards instead of a statement credit.

    Recent findings suggest that generally speaking, Citi Shop clashes with other shopping portals. Both work by referring and tracking your purchase, so they can be mutually exclusive. You'll need to make your purchase through whichever offer is better.

    Related: Chase shopping portal guide: How to earn bonus Ultimate Rewards points.

    Unless Citi Shop finds a promo code, it won't lower your total at checkout. Its returns arrive later as statement credits and may require patiently waiting two to six months, sometimes longer.

    Even though you need an eligible Citi card to enroll, you don’t have to pay with it. Citi allows any payment method accepted by the merchant.

    According to recent reports, I really appreciate the flexibility to choose the best card for each purchase. For electronics, I might pick a card with an extended warranty while I might stick to a travel rewards credit card for hotel bookings. You can even pay with a gift card if you wish.

    Regardless of how you pay, the statement credit will post to the Citi card you enrolled.

    Recent findings suggest that if you have an eligible Citi card but rarely remember to click through a shopping portal, Citi Shop is an easy win. Install it, activate offers when the pop-up appears and let the credits come to you. That convenience can also be a big benefit if you have partners or other family members who aren't as motivated to strategize on rewards as you are.

    Recent findings suggest that but with a little extra effort, you might be able to earn even more. When the Citi Shop pop-up appears with an offer, take a minute to compare before you click Activate.

    Checking a shopping portal aggregator such as Cashback Monitor reveals payouts from multiple cash-back, airline and credit card portals, making it easier to compare a Citi Shop statement credit with points or miles elsewhere.

    Sources indicate that suppose a $200 jacket is marked down to $160. Citi Shop finds a $10 coupon, bringing the checkout price to $150, and offers 8% back. Assuming the full amount qualifies, you'd receive a $12 Citi Shop credit. If you pay with a card that earns 2% back and has an activated merchant offer for $5 off a $100 purchase, you'd collect another $8. After all the credits and rewards post, your net cost would be $130.

    Read the terms before getting too excited. Some brands, products, gift cards or coupon codes may be excluded and you might not be able to stack every layer every time. Still, you can often use multiple discounts simultaneously for a better deal.

    Recent findings suggest that citi Shop is not a program for instant gratification. Citi claims statement credits post 61 to 180 days after a completed purchase, though some can take longer.

    According to recent reports, in many cases, offers may show as pending long before they officially pay out, to account for potential returns. Hotel rewards may remain pending until after the stay. Eventually, you'll see it on your statement as "CITI SHOP STATEMENT CREDIT.".

    If a credit hasn't posted after the expected window, contact Citi using the number on the back of your enrolled card. You may want to keep good records along the way, like a screenshot of the offer and an e-receipt from the purchase.

    In a recent development, citi Shop's biggest advantage is convenience. It does the heavy lifting by reminding you to activate offers so you don't miss out on earnings from your online orders, while testing coupon codes along the way. The offers themselves may or may not be the highest available, but they are certainly the easiest.

    To truly optimize your returns, you'll want to compare Citi Shop earnings with those from other shopping portals — and stack other forms of saving along the way. But when that sounds like too much, the ease of this extension can still be a great way to tack on some extra returns.

    • Sources indicate that if you spend a lot at supermarkets and want to earn cash back, the Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express is hard to beat.
    • In this post, I’ll cover the welcome offer, the bonus categories and how they work, the Disney streaming credit, and how this card compares to other options like the no annual fee Blue Cash Everyday® Card from American Express and the Citi Strata Premier® Card.
    • Link: Learn more about the Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that if you spend a lot at supermarkets and want to earn cash back, the Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express is hard to beat. The card offers 6% cash back at U.S. supermarkets and on select streaming subscriptions, which can add up fast for families and anyone with a few monthly subscriptions.

    In this post, I’ll cover the welcome offer, the bonus categories and how they work, the Disney streaming credit, and how this card compares to other options like the no annual fee Blue Cash Everyday® Card from American Express and the Citi Strata Premier® Card.

    Link: Learn more about the Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express.

    Before I get into the Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card review, here’s a quick look at the most crucial features and fees:.

    And here are my thoughts on the main pros and cons of the Blue Cash Preferred Card:.

    In a recent development, when applying for a credit card, obviously the welcome offer, the eligibility, and the fees, are major considerations, given that they can be the first factors that impact interest in a card. So along those lines, let’s take a look at those details for the Amex Blue Cash Preferred.

    The Amex Blue Cash Preferred is currently offering the following welcome bonus: You may be eligible for as high as $300 cash back after spending $3,000 in purchases on your latest Card in the first 6 months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer. Cash back is received as Reward Dollars, redeemable for statement credit or for other select options. Terms Apply.

    In a recent development, that’s a solid bonus for a card at this price point, and the six month window gives you plenty of time to hit the spending requirement. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

    Sources indicate that amex cards tend to be fairly easy to get approved for if you have excellent credit. A few rules to know:.

    Sources indicate that as you can see, this card is marketed as offering a bonus “as high as” a certain amount. The way this works, you can apply for the Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card, and then find out your offer amount. Then you can decide whether you want to accept the offer or not. That’s an unconventional approach for a welcome offer. At least Amex has the “apply with confidence” feature, so there won’t be a hard pull unless you accept the offer.

    It has been revealed that the Amex Blue Cash Preferred has a $0 intro annual fee for the first year, then $95. (Rates & Fees). That puts it in line with other mid-range cards. No first year annual fee is a nice perk, as it lets you test the card and see how much value you’re getting before you commit to the ongoing fee.

    If you decide the card isn’t working for you after the first year, you can always downgrade to the no annual fee Blue Cash Everyday Card.

    You can add authorized users to the card at no extra cost, so that their spending can help you rack up rewards.

    Recent findings suggest that I wouldn’t recommend using the Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card outside the U.S. or for purchases in foreign currencies. The 2.7% foreign transaction fee will eat into your rewards (Rates & Fees). There are plenty of other cards with no foreign transaction fees that are better suited for international spending.

    The Amex Blue Cash Preferred has some excellent bonus categories, especially if you spend a lot at U.S. supermarkets and on streaming. Below is a full breakdown.

    In a recent development, this is the headline feature of the Amex Blue Cash Preferred, and it’s the single best cash back rate for U.S. supermarket spending that I’m aware of. You earn 6% cash back at U.S. supermarkets on up to $6,000 per year in purchases (then 1%). This is the only bonus category with an earning cap.

    According to recent reports, to put that in perspective, if you spend $500 a month on U.S. supermarket spending, you’d earn $360 per year in cash back from this category alone. That more than covers the $95 annual fee.

    Note that supermarkets don’t include superstores, warehouse clubs (like Costco or Sam’s Club), or discount stores. If most of your grocery shopping happens at a traditional supermarket, this card is incredibly rewarding.

    The Amex Blue Cash Preferred also offers 6% cash back on select U.S. streaming subscriptions. The list of qualifying services is quite long and includes most of the major platforms: Netflix, Hulu, Disney+, ESPN+, HBO Max, Spotify, Apple TV, Apple Music, Amazon Music Unlimited, YouTube Premium, YouTube TV, Peacock, Sling TV, and many more.

    If you’re spending $50 to $100 a month across streaming services (which many households are these days), that 6% adds up nicely.

    The Amex Blue Cash Preferred offers 3% cash back on transit purchases, including taxis, ridesharing, parking, tolls, trains, and buses. If you commute by public transit or use rideshare services regularly, this is a solid bonus category.

    Industry observers note that with the Amex Blue Cash Preferred, you also earn 3% cash back at eligible U.S. gas stations, with no caps. Note that this doesn’t include gas purchased at superstores, supermarkets, or warehouse clubs that sell fuel.

    For purchases that don’t fall into the bonus categories, you earn 1% cash back. This is the one weak spot of the card. At just 1% on non-bonused spending, you’ll want to pair this card with something that earns a better return on everyday purchases (more on that below).

    According to recent reports, with the Amex Blue Cash Preferred, you earn Reward Dollars that can be redeemed as statement credits, and there’s no minimum cash back balance required before you can redeem. It’s simple and straightforward, though it’s worth knowing that you can’t use cash back to pay your minimum payment due.

    Sources indicate that as is the case for any credit card, it’s also vital to consider the benefits and credits offered, if any. The Amex Blue Cash Preferred has a reasonable annual fee, so what are the benefits like? Well, they’re potentially pretty solid, and can help justify the annual fee….

    Recent findings suggest that the Amex Blue Cash Preferred offers up to $10 back per month ($120 per year) as a statement credit when you use your enrolled card to purchase a subscription, including a bundle subscription, on DisneyPlus.com, Hulu.com, or Stream.ESPN.com U.S. websites, with no minimum purchase requirement. Subscription is subject to auto-renewal. (Enrollment required).

    Another Amex Blue Cash Preferred benefit is access to Amex Presale Tickets® and Amex Reserved Tickets®, which can come in handy if you’re trying to score tickets to an in-demand concert or sporting event.

    The Amex Blue Cash Preferred also includes an introductory 0% APR offer that can give you some breathing room on purchases and balance transfers.

    In a recent development, enjoy 0% intro APR on purchases and balance transfers for 12 months from the date of account opening. After that, your APR will be a variable APR of 19.74% - 28.74%.

    In a recent development, this could be helpful if you need to transfer an existing credit card balance and have some time to pay it off before interest kicks in, or if you need some extra time to pay off a significant upcoming purchase. Just make sure you pay off your balance in full before the intro period ends, or you’ll be on the hook for interest after all.

    Industry observers note that one benefit that doesn’t get enough attention is the Amex Offers program. This gives you access to targeted deals with a variety of retailers, just by registering your card and making an eligible purchase.

    Different Amex cards get different offers, so having multiple Amex cards in your wallet means more chances to save. Across my Amex cards, this program saves me hundreds of dollars per year.

    According to recent reports, the Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card has fewer travel protections than more premium Amex cards, but it does come with coverage to protect your rental car when you charge the rental to this card. The coverage applies for eligible damage or theft, and it’s secondary, so it kicks in after your own car insurance. There are some exclusions, and it doesn’t include liability coverage, so check your card benefits guide for the full details.

    Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc.

    The Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card offers the following benefits when you shop with the card:.

    These are all helpful benefits that you hopefully won’t have to use (though they do provide some peace of mind). Just remember you need to purchase the relevant items with your card to get this coverage.

    Purchase Protection is an embedded benefit of your Card Membership and requires no enrollment. It can help protect Covered Purchases made on your Eligible Card when they’re accidentally damaged, stolen, or lost, for up to 90 days from the Covered Purchase date. The coverage is limited to up to $10,000 per occurrence, up to $50,000 per Card Member account per calendar year. Coverage Limits Apply. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Firm. When an American Express® Card Member charges a Covered Purchase to an Eligible Card, Extended Warranty§ can provide up to one extra year added to the Original Manufacturer’s Warranty. Applies to warranties of five (5) years or less. Coverage is up to the actual amount charged to your Card for the item up to a maximum of $10,000; not to exceed $50,000 per Card Member account per calendar year. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

    I tend to lean toward points-earning cards for my own spending, but I totally get why a lot of people prefer cash back. It’s simple, flexible, and you can spend it however you want, including on travel. For that crowd, the Blue Cash Preferred is one of the best options out there.

    If you’re someone who is looking to earn cash back and spends a lot at supermarkets, then the Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card is an exceptional choice, in my opinion — 6% cash back will add up quickly.

    The 6% cash back on streaming, and 3% cash back on transit and gas stations, will add up rapidly as well, and up to $120 Disney streaming credit could be worth more than the annual fee.

    Recent findings suggest that however, this isn’t the card I would be using for your everyday spending, as you’d only earn 1% cash back in the categories that aren’t eligible for bonuses. So I’d acquire this card specifically with the intent of using it in the categories offering bonuses.

    So, let’s take a look at what other cards you should potentially be considering.

    If you like the idea of an Amex cash back card but aren’t sure about paying an annual fee, the Blue Cash Everyday Card from American Express (learn more) is the no annual fee alternative where you can earn as high as $200 cash back after spending $2,000 in purchases on your new Card in the first six months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer. Cash back is received as Reward Dollars, redeemable for statement credit or for other select options. Terms Apply.

    Here’s how the two Blue Cash cards compare:.

    According to recent reports, in my opinion, the Blue Cash Preferred is well worth the annual fee if you spend a meaningful amount at supermarkets. The jump from 3% to 6% on U.S. supermarkets adds up fast. If you spend $500 a month at supermarkets, that extra 3% earns you $180 more per year, which nearly doubles the annual fee.

    The Blue Cash Everyday does have one unique advantage: 3% cash back on U.S. online retail purchases, which the Preferred doesn’t offer. If you do a lot of online shopping and less grocery shopping, the Everyday could actually come out ahead.

    The good news is that you can always start with the Blue Cash Preferred and downgrade to the Blue Cash Everyday after the first year if the math doesn’t work out.

    If you’re just looking for the simplest cash back credit card, it’s tough to go wrong with the Citi Double Cash® Card (learn more). The card offers 1% cash back when you make a purchase, and 1% cash back when you pay for that purchase, for a total of 2% back on every purchase. That’s a solid return on everyday spending, and you don’t have to keep track of any bonus spending categories.

    If you’re deciding between the Blue Cash Preferred and a mid-range card from another issuer, the $95 annual fee Citi Strata Premier Card (learn more) is worth considering. These two cards serve pretty different purposes, but they’re at the same price point:.

    The Blue Cash Preferred wins on supermarkets and streaming, hands down. If those are your biggest spending categories, the Blue Cash Preferred is the better card.

    The Strata Premier is the more well-rounded card overall. It earns 3x points across five major categories (dining, gas, supermarkets, airfare, hotels), has no foreign transaction fees, and its ThankYou points can be transferred to airline and hotel partners for potentially much more than face value. If you travel or eat out a lot, the Strata Premier likely comes out ahead.

    Industry observers note that one final card worth considering alongside the Blue Cash Preferred Card is the American Express® Gold Card (learn more). It has a significantly higher annual fee, but it’s unbeatable for earning rewards at U.S. supermarkets — you’ll earn transferable Membership Rewards points too, rather than cash back.

    Here’s a look at how they compare:.

    The Blue Cash Preferred is the best cash back card for supermarket spending, and it’s not particularly close. If groceries and streaming are a significant part of your monthly budget, this card can deliver serious returns, especially with the 6% rate on both categories plus the Disney streaming credit.

    Sources indicate that the annual fee pays for itself quickly if you’re spending even a moderate amount at supermarkets. Pair it with a card like the Citi Double Cash for your non-bonused spending, and you’ve got a strong cash back setup.

    Just keep in mind that the 1% rate on everyday purchases means this card works best as a specialist, not your only card. Use it where it shines, and let a flat-rate card handle the rest.
