    #88696. Will the midterms live up to the hype? 6 key stories we’re watching

    📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1348 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

    Will the midterms live up to the hype? 6 key stories we’re watching

    📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1348 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Across the country, voters are making their way to the polls in the climax of a vitriolic midterm election cycle set against the backdrop of an electorate souring on Donald Trump and Republicans.
    • It has been revealed that each election is billed as being consequential; this one lives up to the hype.
    • A tsunami, a trickle — or something in the middle?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Across the country, voters are making their way to the polls in the climax of a vitriolic midterm election cycle set against the backdrop of an electorate souring on Donald Trump and Republicans. Inflation is up, consumer confidence is down, gas and diesel prices are through the roof, largely due to the president’s war of choice in Iran. The cruelty of his MAGA agenda has roiled the country and left a bad taste even in the mouths of some of his erstwhile supporters.

    It has been revealed that each election is billed as being consequential; this one lives up to the hype. As we await the results, it’s worth taking note of several questions:.

    A tsunami, a trickle — or something in the middle? All are possible, but signs are pointing to significant Democratic gains, likely up to 25 seats in the House, as well as a Senate majority. Dr. Abdul El-Sayed looks increasingly likely to win in Michigan, and James Talarico has Democratic hopes up in Texas. Senate races in Maine, Kansas, Iowa and Alaska are in play, and it’s worth keeping an eye on South Carolina, Mississippi and Louisiana as well.

    Recent findings suggest that one sign will come at 6 p.m. when polls close in Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District, where Democrat Zach Dembo is facing off against Republican Ralph Alvarado. Once a Democratic stronghold, the seat went Republican in 2012 and, despite a close call in 2018, has remained in GOP hands since. Although the district has been gerrymandered to favor Republicans, the energy on the ground is with Dembo. If he posts and maintains a healthy lead, look for significant Democratic gains to unfold throughout the night.

    What effect did redistricting have on the GOP’s chances?

    The midterms will be the first test of the GOP’s redistricting strategy, which saw the party redraw congressional districts in Florida, Texas and other states, partly in response to the gains Trump made with Black and Latino voters in 2024. But polls show those margins have been largely erased as the electorate has turned on the president after nearly two tumultuous years in office, while Democratic legislatures in California and Virginia have imposed their own gerrymanders. According to a Politico poll, the GOP increasingly sees the coalition that returned Trump to office as “crumbling,” and may have gained little or nothing from all this adventurous map-drawing.

    Will progressives be bolstered or chastened?

    Industry observers note that losses — or even narrow wins — by progressive candidates could be used as more evidence by the party’s establishment wing of the need to tack toward the middle ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Larger wins would provide rocket fuel to the movement.

    According to recent reports, the size of the blue wave could well come to be seen as a measure of progressives’ influence and power within the Democratic Party. Losses — or even narrow wins — by progressive candidates could be used as more evidence by the party’s establishment wing of the need to tack toward the middle ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Larger wins — and victories in unexpected places, such as Michigan’s 7th Congressional District where William Lawrence, co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, stands a real chance of unseating incumbent Republican Tom Barrett — would provide rocket fuel to the movement.

    Progressive groups are already on the offensive, getting a head start on spinning tonight’s election results, particularly in anticipation of a narrow El-Sayed win in Michigan. “Expect to hear narrow victories cited as evidence of weak electability,” a Progressive Change Campaign Committee memo obtained by Politico reads. “But a candidate’s first winning margin is not their electoral ceiling.”.

    Will the Haley Stevens drama matter in Michigan?

    Haley Stevens, the Democratic congresswoman who narrowly lost to El-Sayed in Michigan’s Senate primary, has brought the drama in the race’s closing days. As late as Saturday night, she pledged to colleagues and friends that she was backing El-Sayed, only to turn up hours later at a church service with his Republican opponent Mike Rogers, and endorse the former congressman in a video. The cold-dish move has virtually drowned out El-Sayed’s closing message, with Stevens being formally kicked out of the Michigan Democratic Party.

    The question now is if any of it will matter, especially in light of a New York Times/Siena poll taken before Stevens’ move that revealed El-Sayed leading Rogers by 11 points. Michigan Republicans seem to think it won’t, telling Politico they wish the congresswoman had crossed the aisle earlier. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report agrees, moving the race in their ratings to “Leans Democratic,” a shift that was already in the works before Stevens detonated her bomb.

    Still, the results in the state’s Democratic primary were far narrower than the polls indicated, with El-Sayed besting Stevens by only 1%, or 14,893 votes.

    Will Elon Musk get his money’s worth?

    The New York Times reported yesterday that the world’s first trillionaire has dropped a staggering $474 million this election cycle, an historic first. The amount has been spread out across a variety of groups, PACs and funds, but it doesn’t include the “dark-money donations” the Times reports he has also made. Most of the $168 million he contributed to the Senate Leadership Fund has served to shore up Ken Paxton, the GOP nominee for Senate in Texas, who is locked in a tight race with Talarico.

    Musk has a lot riding on Tuesday’s results. Beyond the simple math of whether he got enough bang for his buck, there is also the issue of what will surely face him in the event of a Democratic congressional majority: investigations.

    Recent findings suggest that musk has a lot riding on Tuesday’s results. Beyond the simple math of whether he got enough bang for his buck, there is also the concern of what will surely face him in the event of a Democratic congressional majority: investigations. If the blue wave materializes, Musk can expect congressional inquiries of his activities, including his reported interventions in Russia’s war against Ukraine and his leadership of DOGE during the early months of Trump’s second administration.

    Each election brings surprises. Think not one but both of Georgia’s Senate seats going to Democrats in 2020, or Republicans making big gains in Upcoming York two years later.

    This is the year we could hear the echo of Georgia’s 2020 election results in another Southern state. Despite boasting large Black populations, Senate seats in South Carolina, Mississippi and Louisiana have long been out of reach for Democrats. But there is now a path to victory for the party’s candidates in each of those states.

    Industry observers note that in South Carolina, the GOP incumbent Darline Graham, who was appointed to the seat at Donald Trump’s command following the death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, has proven to be a lackluster candidate, alarming even some Republicans with her performance in debates and on the stump. Democrat Annie Andrews has run a more nimble campaign, and between Graham’s performance and the national state of affairs, she appears to have narrowed the gap.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    Recent findings suggest that mississippi’s incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith has also run a lazy campaign, expecting to coast to victory. But the national political environment under Trump, coupled with campaign gaffes, large Black turnout in the aftermath of the Supreme Court’s decision to gut the Voting Rights Act and clever campaigning by Scott Colom, her Democratic opponent, have helped to put the race in play.

    Louisiana is also a wild card. The state, which is one-third African American, has also seen a surge in early voting among Black residents, and according to a recent poll, the race between Republican Julia Letlow and Democrat Jamie Davis, who is Black, is tied.

    It has been revealed that polls are not predictive. The political history of these states continues to favor Republicans, but any of them could deliver one of 2026’s electoral surprises. If that happens, it will signal that the blue wave has become a blue tsunami.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a latest majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec.
    • That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    Senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a latest majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec. 1.

    That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.

    The prospect of an earlier vote had been floated as a way to prevent internal divisions from hobbling the incoming majority before the 120th Congress even began.

    But supporters of Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., both in the chamber and among party activists outside it, were increasingly casting the idea of a shorter contest as a bid to halt momentum for his bid against Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

    Even as Schumer maintained that he has the votes necessary to be elected as majority leader, several senators insisted Tuesday the discussion taking place within the caucus was a good thing.

    Sources indicate that “I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday following the conference’s lunch.

    Van Hollen for his part told reporters Tuesday he believes his bid has “momentum at this point in time, which is why there was an effort to short-circuit the process.”.

    “And fortunately, I think that will fail.”.

    Several senators leaving the meeting remarked the topic of the leadership contest did not come up at all, and that neither Van Hollen nor Schumer gave a presentation regarding their bids.

    Recent findings suggest that that was in large part due to the absence of the incoming senators — which could be as high as 13, depending on how the dust settles in Alaska — who are able to vote in the leadership elections. Retiring senators do not cast a ballot.

    With such a large class of incoming freshman, several incumbents saw it crucial to keep the election scheduled as is.

    “No one has ever raised that with me. I mean, I saw a rumor that some were wanting to contemplate that,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Tuesday after the meeting. “The leadership discussions did not come up today. And part of the reason is we didn’t have the newcomers.”.

    “Remember, they all get a vote in the leadership discussion, and it would be hard to get them here,” Kaine continued, noting that only Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., was present for Tuesday’s lunch amid his belated orientation. “But nobody else was here, and that discussion needs to have the newcomers because newcomers get votes. The outgoers don’t, right?”.

    Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. echoed that sentiment on Monday evening, saying, “I want to hear from the freshman class as well.”.

    Sen. Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, stated, “I don’t know that” when asked about moving up the elections. “I think that we need to make sure that there’s enough time for what I would call a robust discussion about what we’re going to do. I think we should be very embracing of the new people who have been through fire to get here, and I think that we have to make sure that all these voices are heard.

    “They’ve got a lot of talent to bring to the table,” she said.

    Several senators-elect are among those who have publicly thrown their hats into Van Hollen’s corner, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.El-Sayed on Tuesday said at The Atlantic Summit that he sees Van Hollen as “unique” in his experience in the Senate and running the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee as well as what he called “a willingness to take risks.”.

    Industry observers note that “We need people who are willing to take legislative risk,” he said. “We need to rethink the way we legislate. It just should not be the process where you make one or two omnibus pieces of legislation that nobody really knows what’s in them,” he continued, advocating for piecemeal legislation.

    It has been revealed that but there are about 15 Democrats who have publicly backed Schumer’s bid. If former Rep. Mary Peltola maintains her lead in the lone outstanding Senate race in Alaska, Schumer would need 29 to secure the helm of the ship.

    Industry observers note that “I committed to Sen. Schumer literally months ago, and I continue to support him,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said Monday. “I’m incredibly excited about the fresh ideas that our new colleagues have, and their energy, and the potential for changing the way we operate in the Senate, which we have to do because we need to be more effective.”.

    It has been revealed that several incumbents have also thrown their support behind Van Hollen for leadership change, including Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.“I think, as I’ve noted many times, the American people want change in the way we do business here in Washington, and I think Chris Van Hollen would be a great leader of the Democrats,” Sanders said Monday.

    Several senators and senators-elect are refusing to comment publicly on who they’ll back.

    According to recent reports, that included Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., who mentioned he wants “to hear the commitments from folks that are pursuing this leadership role as well as every leadership position in the Senate, as well as chairs of committees, to what their commitments are to having a strong agenda that’s going to improve people’s lives.”.

    According to recent reports, kaine is also in that camp, and insisted Monday he hadn’t made up his mind. But he did speak positively of Schumer’s recruiting efforts in the midterms and history of dealing with a Trump White House.

    “Schumer just delivered a major win for us. No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer,” he said. “Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anybody else in the caucus, and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge over the next few years.”.

    According to recent reports, “The voters are also overwhelmingly demanding change,” he stated. “So we got to figure that out as a caucus, and we’re going to be able to. And we’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats. We like democracy.”.

    Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., also remained mum on who he’ll support but stated, “You can’t argue” Schumer brought Democrats the majority.

    “I think it’s a healthy thing to try and improve how the conference goes about its business,” he said. “I don’t think that is a distraction. We can deal with some distractions. We have to keep our eye on the ball.”.

    Recent findings suggest that sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who last week called for latest leadership in a news conference with Sanders, days before Van Hollen’s announcement, was noncommittal arriving to the Capitol on Monday if that meant she’d be supporting the Maryland Democrat.

    Senate Democrats’ election will most likely be a secret ballot. And most senators remained unified against moving the leadership elections before they recess for the Thanksgiving break.

    In a recent development, “They should not be moved up. There was a reason that those rule changes took place before, and they should take place in December,” Lujan said.

    Kaine dismissed Van Hollen’s challenge as anything unusual.

    Recent findings suggest that “We’re Democrats. It’s frankly unusual that there usually [aren’t] challenges to Democratic leaders because we’re Democrats,” he mentioned. “It’s been a little unusual to have been here for 13 years and not really have them like this. But I think it’s a discussion not just about the two contenders for the leader role, but also the leadership team and priorities, and it’s all wrapped up in one discussion.”.

    “That’s why we decided, don’t do these votes until December, because you want to let the election settle and understand exactly what’s up, and then hear from potential votes.”.

    Industry observers note that sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said, “I think we should stick with the rules when it comes to the caucus. … That’s going to be what makes sure that we show that we have a real process.”.

    Sanders asked: “Why would anyone want to do that?” when asked.

    “I think there’s a date that’s been called, and that should be the date.”.

    Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

    • Donald Trump just met with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in China for a tripartite global summit — and nobody has any real news to report, except for Trump, so desperate for media attention that he’s giving interviews to anyone holding a hot mic and a video camera.
    • Every periodical you might care to read — even the political or news-based ones — has brought forward its substantial-think “review” of the game, now available on PlayStation and Xbox.
    • Jeffrey Blehar is a National Review staff writer living in Chicago.

    Donald Trump just met with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in China for a tripartite global summit — and nobody has any real news to report, except for Trump, so desperate for media attention that he’s giving interviews to anyone holding a hot mic and a video camera. The lack of news is not just because of a (predictable) blackout enforced by the Chinese Communist Party, but because the collective consciousness of America has shut down for the next few days. If you thought the traditional four-day Thanksgiving Day Weekend was typically slow, get ready for a one-and-a-half-week productivity dip in the economy as the video game Grand Theft Auto VI goes live across the nation. Even National Review, as sober-minded as it is, has more than a few fans of the series on its staff.

    Every periodical you might care to read — even the political or news-based ones — has brought forward its substantial-think “review” of the game, now available on PlayStation and Xbox. For all I know we’ll be publishing one too. But I am not a gamer — not in the modern sense of the word, although I did whip out my copy of Battletoads for the NES the other day to prove that I’ve still “got it” — and this will not be a review of GTA VI. Instead, I want to talk about time spent — and time wasted.

    Jeffrey Blehar is a National Review staff writer living in Chicago. He is also the co-host of National Review’s Political Beats podcast, which explores the great music of the modern era with guests from the political world happy to find something non-political to talk about.

    On “Grand Theft Auto VI and How We Spend Our Time”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that move over, Haley Stevens: There’s a new competitor for the most pathetic reaction to plummeting political fortunes. Elon Musk, the former Trump administration member and the world’s richest man, has seen the midterm election forecast for conservative candidates, and he’s responded by petulantly playing with his toys.

    The X owner started “Anakin-posting” on Monday. The purely online phenomenon finds far-right and MAGA nerds recasting Star Wars’ Anakin Skywalker, the man who will become Darth Vader, as a tragic hero and paragon of traditional values. A typical post uses generative AI to reframe the “Star Wars” films’ genocidal space monk as a masculine, hyper-conservative, attentive father. Musk’s post highlights Anakin, as played by actor Hayden Christensen, sitting on a throne surrounded by his children, Luke and Leia, and his wife, Padme. The AI illustration has pulled liberally from all three trilogies, placing the adult faces of Mark Hamill and Carrie Fisher on the children. Natalie Portman’s Padme appears to be wearing her makeup and crown from “Black Swan.” The Sith first family is surrounded by 1970s-era storm troopers and 2010s imperial guards.

    “This is what they stole from us,” Musk captioned the computer-generated photo of his sci-fi fan fiction.

    For the unfamiliar, Anakin was a member of an order of space knights. As a young man, he began having prophetic dreams of his wife dying in childbirth. Consumed by ambition and anger, and desperate to avoid the fate he envisioned, he was manipulated by several elderly politicians into betraying his chivalric order, killing many of his fellow knights and slaughtering an entire school full of squires for fear of retribution. Unable to save his wife, and grievously injured from a battle with his former mentor, he became a running dog of a fascist empire that aimed to rule the entire galaxy.

    Right-wing young men have warped that story through the established MAGA lens of “returning to tradition,” picturing a world where having the conviction to kill a bunch of toddlers is celebrated.

    In a recent development, the typical example of “Anakin-posting” expresses rage at a stagnant economy or lack of prospects by sharing images of Christensen’s Anakin looking stoic. MAGA influencers like Jack Posobiec have added a dash of intergalactic racism, sharing images of a young Anakin surrounded by literal aliens to hint at a pro-segregationist message. Others have reimagined Anakin’s mentors as chiding liberal scolds, grafting pink hair and a keffiyeh onto Obi-Wan Kenobi. In the pathetic galaxy of Gen Z men, anything from mid-century magazine ads to a Disney-owned sci-fi epic for children can be a stand in for their cultural grievances.

    Recent findings suggest that enough time has passed between the prequels and the present that Anakin can be presented as a brooding badass. The primary criticism of the movies at the time concerned Christensen’s portrayal of Anakin as a whiny child throwing a deadly tantrum. The knotty and boring political intrigue subplots of the films have been forgotten, making it easy to gloss over Anakin being a stooge for politicians playing a game beyond his ken.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    Musk, in particular, does have reasons to empathize with the “Star Wars” villain. After believing he had found a way to reshape the government toward his own ends via DOGE, he was booted when the program proved deeply unpopular. Seeing visions of a blue wave washout, he used his financial superpower to try and avoid what appears to be an oncoming loss. Separated from the levers of power and now half a billion dollars poorer, Musk has been forced to play-act a scenario where he won. His image-generating toy gave him the happy ending that politics, relationships and wealth couldn’t.

    Industry observers note that but all the AI bots can’t undo the facts of Anakin’s story. He was ultimately killed by the evil emperor he served, dying in front of the son he abandoned. His “return to tradition” was a last-minute awakening, when he was forced to confront all the harm he had done and the miserable life he had led. Now there’s something for Musk to aspire to.

    Former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov. 3. (Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images).

    Industry observers note that former Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, giving Senate Democrats their ninth pickup of the midterm elections and bringing their caucus’s total seats in the next Congress to 56.

    Industry observers note that the Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, a full two weeks after Election Day. The latest tranche of ballots counted put the former congresswoman past the 50-percent threshold to win the election outright without Alaska’s ranked choice voting system kicking in.

    With her victory, Peltola, who is Yup’ik, becomes one of the first Native American women elected to the Senate, along with fellow Democrat Peggy Flanagan, who won the open seat in Minnesota this month.

    “As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first.,” Peltola noted in a statement after the race was called.

    The Alaska race was the final Senate contest to be called in a midterm election that saw Democrats win commanding majorities in both chambers of Congress. Besides Alaska, Democrats also flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi.

    According to recent reports, peltola, a former state legislator, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election for the state’s at-large district. She comfortably won the general election that fall but was narrowly unseated in 2024 by Republican Nick Begich.

    According to recent reports, she entered the Senate contest in January, positioning herself as an independent-minded Democrat and invoking the legacies of two well-liked Alaska Republicans, the late Sen. Ted Stevens and the late Rep. Don Young, whom she succeeded in the House.

    She campaigned on the slogan “fish, family, freedom” and played up her moderate views and deep roots in the state.

    It has been revealed that but the race was marked by allegations of political gamesmanship. In addition to the incumbent Sullivan, a retired colonel in the U.S. Marine Corps Reserves, the Senate ballot also included a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan. The Fresh York Times reported late last month that operatives aligned with Peltola’s campaign were involved in the effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan in an attempt to confuse voters.

    Peltola has said she had no connection to the scheme.

    Prior to Election Day, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the result if Sen. Sullivan were to lose. The lawsuit was tossed earlier this month by a federal judge.

    Trump also suggested that all votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan should be added to the incumbent’s total. “If you add them up, Dan Sullivan wins,” the president told reporters Monday. But as of Tuesday evening when the race was called, Peltola had more votes than both Sullivans combined.

    The Alaska race was initially viewed as a long shot for Democrats. The Last Frontier has elected a Democratic senator just once in the past 50 years – in 2008, when Mark Begich ousted Stevens. Begich, the Democratic uncle of the current Republican congressman, served a single term before he was ousted by Sullivan in 2014.

    But anger in Alaska over the rising cost of food and fuel — already among the highest in the nation — provided Democrats with an opening.

    According to recent reports, "56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer noted in a statement Tuesday night. "But I knew if we concentrated on getting the best candidates, and if we focused like a laser on the costs, corruption, and chaos that Donald Trump has wrought throughout America, we would have shot.".

    In other Alaska races, Democrats flipped the governor’s mansion, with former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins winning an open-seat race to become the first Democrat elected governor of the state since Tony Knowles won a second term in 1998.

    The race for the state’s at-large House district will be decided by ranked choice voting, with tabulations expected to take place Wednesday. Begich, the GOP incumbent, was leading Tuesday with 47.5 percent of the vote and is expected to prevail over independent Bill Hill, who had the backing of national Democrats and trailed with 42 percent. Another Democrat and a Libertarian combined for the remainder of the vote.

Marsha Blackburn to appoint him to her Senate seat if, as expected, she wins the Tennessee governor’s race this week. Having a Senate seat would not only prevent impeachment; it could make prosecuting him for alleged war crimes much harder as well.

His children are deeply involved in the family business as well. And as the Epstein report made sure to note, some of the crimes Trump and his associates have been accused of committing with his old friend Epstein carry no statute of limitations.

    We need your help to stay independent.

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of Latest York or Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia — have been highly focused weeding out MAGA corruption.

    Sen. Jon Ossoff easily defeated a challenge from Republican Rep. Mike Collins to hold on to his Georgia Senate seat on Tuesday, according to AP projections.

    After Donald Trump carried the state in 2024, early forecasts predicted tough sledding for Ossoff. But during a brutal government shutdown — the longest on record — the senator signaled he was willing to stake his candidacy on protecting Affordable Care Act subsidies, and he proved an adept campaigner who was hyper-focused on Georgia issues. Ossoff focused his stump speeches around affordability, skyrocketing inflation and foreign entanglements, hammering Trump for his costly war with Iran.

    For his part, Collins’ candidacy was hamstrung by controversies involving his payroll and affiliation with alleged white nationalists.

    In a recent development, frequently floated as a 2028 contender, Ossoff adopted a fighter’s stance at his campaign events. Like feisty Michigan candidate Abdul El-Sayed, the senator took every opportunity to land a jab against Republicans, occasionally causing some monocle-popping among centrist commentators still holding on to the idea of the dignity of the presidential office.     💡 Key Takeaways
    • Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms defeated Republican billionaire Rick Jackson in Georgia‘s gubernatorial election Tuesday, becoming the first Black woman elected governor in American history and ending more than two decades of Republican control of the state’s highest office.
    • In a recent development, the contest pitted two sharply different candidates to succeed term-limited Republican Gov.
    • Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor and adviser to President Joe Biden, campaigned on expanding access to health care, improving public education and addressing the rising cost of living.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms defeated Republican billionaire Rick Jackson in Georgia‘s gubernatorial election Tuesday, becoming the first Black woman elected governor in American history and ending more than two decades of Republican control of the state’s highest office.

    In a recent development, the contest pitted two sharply different candidates to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Brian Kemp, whose departure opened the governor’s office for the first time in eight years.

    Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor and adviser to President Joe Biden, campaigned on expanding access to health care, improving public education and addressing the rising cost of living. Jackson, a billionaire health care executive and political newcomer, emphasized cutting taxes, reducing government spending and bringing his private-sector experience to state government.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    Jackson invested more than $200 million of his own money into the campaign, making his bid one of the most expensive self-funded gubernatorial campaigns in American history.

    The election also ended Republicans’ decades-long control of Georgia’s governorship. The last Democrat elected governor was Roy Barnes in 1998. Barnes lost his reelection bid to Republican Sonny Perdue in 2002, and Republicans have held the office since Perdue took office in January 2003.

    Georgia’s changing political landscape added another dimension to the contest. Once a reliably Republican state in presidential elections, Georgia narrowly backed Democrat Joe Biden in 2020 before returning to President Donald Trump in 2024. Democrats also captured both U.S. Senate seats in 2021, with Raphael Warnock subsequently winning a full term in 2022.

    In a recent development, on Tuesday, Georgia voters also reelected Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, demonstrating the state’s continued willingness to support Democrats in statewide contests.

    Bottoms is the first Black governor elected in Georgia, the first woman to hold the state’s highest office and the first Black woman elected governor anywhere in the United States. She is also the first Democrat to win Georgia’s governorship in 28 years, breaking a Republican winning streak dating back to 2002.

    • According to recent reports, britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority.
    • Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S.
    • The draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    A bill introduced by Sen. Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S. effort to fight it.

    The draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts. It is aimed at ensuring that federal agencies, law enforcement, financial institutions, telecommunications and technology companies and other groups work together, according to an overview from Britt.

    The new office would promote intelligence sharing across the public and private sectors, coordinate consumer education efforts and improve assistance for victims.

    Britt, R-Ala., noted the effort is needed because fraudsters operate nimbly utilizing social media while taking advantage of fragmented or disorganized responses from individual companies and government agencies.

    In a recent development, “This effort is about bringing everyone to the table and making sure our response keeps pace with the criminals who are exploiting upcoming technologies and gaps between sectors,” she mentioned in a statement. “When we work together to identify threats earlier and share information more effectively, we can better protect American families and businesses.”.

    The office would develop a “lexicon of fraud” so that terms for different kinds of scams are standardized between various federal law enforcement agencies to promote a “whole-of-government response,” a Britt aide said.

    According to recent reports, the office also would work to broaden the approach to combating fraud beyond just having financial institutions reimburse victims. It would tap telecommunications and technology companies to address fraud at its source, such as rip-offs that start as text messages, social media posts or online advertisements.

    In a recent development, britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. She is the sponsor of a bill that would allow state, local and tribal law enforcement agencies to use federal grant funding to investigate financial fraud, particularly scams targeted at the elderly.

    The measure highlights the prevalence of "pig butchering," a common technique where a predator cultivates a personal relationship with a victim over many months to extract the most cash.

    The House passed its version of the bill in September with overwhelming bipartisan support. The House sponsor is Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa.

    Sources indicate that senior financial abuse also was the focus of a bill the House passed in an overwhelming 414-2 vote in June. The legislation, sponsored by Rep. Ann Wagner, R-Mo., would codify Securities and Exchange Commission guidance that permits mutual funds and their agents to postpone the sale of securities if there is a reasonable belief that financial exploitation of someone who is elderly or disabled is occurring.

    It's not clear whether the Senate will take action on these bills or Britt's by the end of the year.

    “If it doesn’t get through in the lame duck, it will continue to be a priority in the 120th [Congress],” the Britt aide said.

Her campaign launch video hinged on measles outbreaks and the harm of anti-vax sentiments at the highest levels of public health. She flubbed softball questions around foreign affairs on the debate stage, a strong suit of her hawkish brother. Her dismal poll numbers pushed Trump to rally for Graham repeatedly in the state, cementing even stronger associations between the Republican nominee and Trump’s unpopular policies.

    According to recent reports, high early turnout among Black voters in the state also spelled trouble for Graham. The community, which is largely Democratic, turned out in high relative numbers and helped swing the race toward Andrews.

    It has been revealed that the Democratic candidate worked to avoid the associations with national party leaders that hamstrung Graham, refraining from appearances with prominent Democrats in the race’s final weeks. Andrews painted herself as a pragmatist, willing to work with national Republicans to score wins for South Carolinians. Late last month, Andrews received a shocking bipartisan endorsement from two former governors of South Carolina. Republican David Beasley joined Democrat Jim Hodges to support Andrews over Trump-backed Graham, saying Andrews was the only candidate focused on “making things better.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    James Talarico, the charismatic Texas state representative who campaigned by talking extensively about his Christian faith, has defeated state Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was Donald Trump’s hand-picked choice, in Tuesday’s most high-profile U.S. Senate race. Late on Tuesday evening, Talarico led by more than a million votes, and the Associated Press called the race just before 11 p.m. Eastern time.

    This marks the first time a Democrat has won a statewide race in Texas since 1994, and another such result, perhaps even more surprising, followed almost immediately. Democrat Gina Hinojosa has won the Texas governor’s race, according to the AP, beating Republican incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott by more than 700,000 votes.

    The big blue wave of 2026 has featured numerous surprising results, including the upset victory by Democrat Annie Andrews over Republican Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina’s Senate race. But these dramatic and unexpected Democratic wins in Texas stand out. The Senate campaign between Talarico and Paxton became one of the most expensive state-level races in American history, and according to CNN analyst David Axelrod, Hinojosa was outspent 10 to one by Abbott. Talarico’s campaign also became a major target for Democratic donors and an opportunity to vent their frustration and anger with Trump’s second presidential term.

    It has been revealed that A combined $573 million were spent by Talarico and Paxton, as well as their defeated primary opponents, over the course of this campaign. Much of that spending was the result of Elon Musk, the world’s richest man. The CEO of SpaceX and Tesla pumped an estimated $474 million into this race, virtually all of it to support Paxton, setting a new record for a single donor in a political campaign. Most of that money was funneled through went to Musk’s personal super PAC, but around $168 million went to the Senate Leadership Fund. Another $10 million went to the pro-Paxton Lone Star Liberty PAC, which spammed voters with AI-generated robocalls attacking Talarico. Meanwhile, Talarico’s campaign and Democratic PACs raised about $133 million.

    Recent findings suggest that although Talarico, like other Democrats, focused on affordability and fighting corruption, he also sought to challenge the dominant view that only Republicans can be devout Christians. His campaign attracted various right-wing conspiracy theories, including claims that he was an emasculated “secret vegan” who suffered from mental illness. Democrats worried that this viral misinformation might overshadow numerous allegations about Paxton, including a Wall Street Journal report that he partied in Dubai with two fugitives from U.S. justice and a woman who wasn’t his wife.

    Sources indicate that although Talarico has led in recent public polls, the size of his victory was unexpected. At this writing, it appears almost certain that Democrats will win the Senate, having already flipped seats in both South Carolina and North Carolina, where former Gov. Roy Cooper easily won the open seat held by outgoing Republican Sen. Thom Tillis. Democrats also lead the Senate races in Iowa, Maine and Ohio, although those races remain undecided.

    Industry observers note that jeffries' nomination followed the election of current Democratic Caucus Vice Chairman Ted Lieu, D-Calif., to serve as the caucus chair in the next Congress. It was a success that, at least in part, led Republicans to launch a national gerrymandering scheme largely thwarted by Democrats, as well as an unfavorable economic climate of the president’s own making.

After more than a year of ICE raids, mass deportations and threats against naturalized citizens, Latinos have swung to the Democrats en masse, playing a decisive role in Talarico’s win. Trump’s attacks on civil rights, immigrants’ rights and the social safety net have cut across demographic groups, and have had a strong negative impact on young voters. Drunk on his own power, the president has spent the better part of two years splintering his own coalition — and giving Democrats an opening they were happy to exploit.

    It has been revealed that senator John Cornyn recently blocked the nomination of the eminently qualified T. Elliot Gaiser to the federal district court in Texas, preferring a favorite-son candidate whom President Trump did not nominate. But the Constitution is clear: The nomination belongs to the president, not the distinguished senator. The constitutional power to “advise and consent” does not belong to a single senator, but to the Senate as a whole. Senator Cornyn’s use of a long-standing privilege conveyed by his colleagues usurps the power of both the president and the Senate.

    According to recent reports, the “blue slip” privilege does not exist in the Constitution or even in the Senate Rules. It is a practice of the Judiciary Committee not to advance a judicial nominee to a vote without the approval of both of the State’s senators. Invented in 1916, its scope and application are entirely within the discretion of the Senate Judiciary chairman, Chuck Grassley. He ought to use his discretion to put Gaiser’s nomination to a vote.

    Dave Yost is senior counsel and vice president of policy innovation at Alliance Defending Freedom. He previously served as the attorney general of Ohio.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Pretend I’m on the ballot, the president of the United States repeatedly told American voters over the last several weeks. Millions of voters did exactly that. Be careful what you wish for, my dude.

    In a recent development, the astonishing results of the 2026 midterm elections do not just represent a rebuke or a political setback for Donald Trump. Those neutral-sounding terms of art are not remotely adequate. This was a historic smackdown, a massive, crushing defeat on a scale suffered by no incumbent president in living memory. It represents this nation’s collective awakening — admittedly rather late in the game — to this individual’s uniquely poisonous effects on our public life and civil society.

    Industry observers note that many larger political questions will emerge from this epic defeat, which will see any and all surviving elected Republicans (not that there are many) scurrying for cover and trying to establish as much distance as possible from Trump. They will lose his number. They will profess that they were never convinced MAGA believers, or that they secretly disagreed with the ICE reign of terror, with the war in Iran, with the disastrous tariffs, with the ideological assault on liberal democracy.

    Is JD Vance still a plausible 2028 presidential contender, having hitched his wagon to this tyrant, who has now been thoroughly pantsed in public and exposed as a pathetic loser? Will Pete Hegseth get even one more opportunity for podcaster-style flexing before the defanged Pentagon press corps? Let’s give Marco Rubio an infinitesimal amount of credit for creeping quietly through the corridors of power and staying out of the headlines. Whether his neocon mouse act is enough to survive the Trumpocalypse moment remains to be seen.

    It has been revealed that in his inimitable style, Trump is already blaming others for this defeat. He has accused Texas Gov. Greg Abbott — who lost his seat to Democrat Gina Hinojosa in one of Tuesday night’s numerous shockers — of being a RINO sellout. As impossible as it is to talk about honor with these people, that is an act of dishonorable treachery, given how eagerly Abbott has crawled and begged and prostrated himself before the Trumpian throne.

    In a recent development, then again, in an ass-backward way, Trump has a point. He didn’t do this all by himself; no one could have managed that. He loaded up the pipe with bigotry and xenophobia and fear and insane conspiracy theories, and adult Republican humans who used to believe in wrong-headed but somewhat sane political doctrines inhaled it all eagerly, persuading themselves that the resulting high would insulate them from the failure of their ideas. It only made the problem worse — all the problems, really — and they should have seen that coming.

    Sources indicate that the president corrupted and enslaved a historic American political party with a complicated but illustrious history, the party of Abraham Lincoln and Ulysses S. Grant and Dwight Eisenhower and Ronald Reagan. I’m not the biggest fan of that party either, but it has certainly had its moments, including the first woman to serve in both houses of Congress and the first Black man elected to the U.S. Senate. Trump insisted that it surrender everything to him — its principles, its history and its soul, if political parties have such a thing — and as in every fable about making a deal with the devil, now it has been destroyed.

    It has been revealed that we don’t know how this election would have turned out in the unimaginable alternate universe where Trump stayed out of it. But he didn’t. He forced Sen. John Cornyn out of the race in Texas, in favor of Ken Paxton. Look what happened. He picked Darline Graham to replace her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, in South Carolina. Look what happened. He picked Mike Collins to run against Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia, and Michael Whatley to run against former Gov. Roy Cooper in North Carolina. Look what happened. He praised Ohio Sen. Jon Husted’s rear end and embraced gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s noxious campaign ad. Look what happened there, too.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    Sources indicate that and that’s without considering the supposedly ingenious MAGA strategy of redistricting congressional seats in one state after another, with the objective of locking in a permanent Republican majority. How will that play out over the longer term? That’s impossible to say, but in 2026 it seems to have unleashed an extraordinary backlash. Forget all the hand-wringing about purple districts and swing districts; the congressional map is a nationwide wipeout. As I write this, the New York Times is predicting a Democratic majority in the House of Representatives of 256 seats. That may or may not hold up, but however this ends, it’s likely to be the biggest midterm swing in more than 30 years.

    Are there still die-hard MAGA Republicans in deep-red exurbs or rural districts who will continue to profess fealty to Trump in the wake of this catastrophe, and perhaps even maintain that it’s all some kind of grand misunderstanding? Yeah, sure. Any cult movement has its true believers and willing sacrifices. Years after his resignation, the postmistress in the rural town where I spent summers as a kid never took down the portrait of Richard Nixon. Then she retired and moved away, someone else took the job and Nixon’s picture wound up out back, in the dumpster.

    In a recent development, that’s about where we are. Trump has always been poisonous. Republicans are finally learning that the hard way.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    President Donald Trump prepares to shake hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China's President Xi Jinping looks on before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa / POOL / AFP via Getty Images).

    Some Senate Democrats have heartburn about President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, but Republicans counter by saying he could get the Russian and Chinese leaders to budge on a list of issues even as he appears politically weakened at home.

    Trump arrived Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen economic zone on the banks of the Pearl River ahead of a high-level summit that was ostensibly slated to focus on paring each countries’ nuclear arsenal. But before he left, Trump signaled the three-way talks also likely would include the artificial intelligence race, Moscow’s bloody war with Ukraine, global trade and his standoff with Iran.

    The U.S. commander in chief’s tendency to sound deferential to Putin and habit of referring to Xi as a personal “friend” concerns many congressional Democrats. But Trump’s GOP allies on Capitol Hill, despite this month’s midterm election losses, still describe him as a dealmaker who has a chance to use his final years to bend Putin and Xi toward U.S. interests.

    Rick Scott, a Florida Republican who sits on the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, noted Tuesday he was hopeful that Trump could make some progress on at least one issue with the Russian and Chinese leaders.

    It has been revealed that “As we all know, China and Russia want to destroy our way of life,” he said. “But it would be great to reduce … nuclear stockpiles and make sure we're not going to ever get attacked.

    Recent findings suggest that still, Scott sounded skeptical about two world leaders Trump has tried to keep close during his two terms. “But do I trust Xi or Putin? No, they're a bunch of liars.” Asked if he worries Trump might trust them too much, Scott replied: “I don't think he trusts him any more than I do. … I'm glad the president's trying. Hope springs eternal. But do I actually really believe something good's going to come out of it? I don't.”.

    Outgoing House Armed Services Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., remarked part of Trump’s talks on Thursday “should be to make sure the world is a safer place, to make sure we don't have aggressive behavior like Russia in an unprovoked attack against Ukraine.

    “They ought to be talking about how they don't do those sorts of things, how they don't threaten their neighbors, how they don't try to intimidate through the assertion of force that they ought to be able to work together to make sure we assure a safe globe,” noted Wittman, who lost his reelection race earlier this month.

    That comment came one day after Trump told reporters as he left the White House for Asia that he sees Putin “backing down a little bit” in his conduct of the war with Ukraine.

    In a recent development, “I think he could be tougher. I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly,” Trump noted Monday. “I think he's backing down.”.

    Those kinds of deferential remarks about the Russian leader are a big reason why some Democrats have heartburn about Thursday’s meeting.

    According to recent reports, senate Armed Services member Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, noted Tuesday that she’s concerned about the Shenzhen summit because “I’m not sure what’s going to pop out of [Trump’s] mouth next — especially for a meeting with two guys he clearly likes.”.

    Recent findings suggest that sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., also a member of the Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, stated he has “high hopes” for the trilateral meeting — but “maybe not high expectations.”.

    Sources indicate that “I have some points of anxiety. I'm nervous about any discussion about Ukraine that doesn't involve the Ukrainians. And, so, some of the advance to this is like, ‘We're going to talk about ending the Ukraine war.’ You can't do that without Ukraine at the table,” Kaine noted. “So the desire to bring about more peace and stability, that's a good thing to talk about. But no conditions about Ukraine and ending that war without them at the table? Not so sure about that.”.

    It has been revealed that during remarks Tuesday on the Senate floor, Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer criticized what he described as Trump’s misplaced priorities.

    “Enforcement of the fresh rules restricting China’s access to our most sensitive AI chips should start today,” the New York Democrat remarked, adding that Trump should focus more of his Asia swing on securing commitments from U.S. allies to block China from gaining an upper hand in the AI technology race.

    Trump touted just that on Tuesday during remarks in Manila at a U.S.-Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in the Philippines.

    “Since I returned to office, we've made major trade deals with Malaysia, Cambodia, Indonesia, as well as Japan, South Korea, and almost everybody, frankly, at the table,” he said. “And we've made many other vital agreements across the region spanning energy, critical minerals and technology.”.

    But on Wednesday, Trump appeared to have pivoted to the trip’s main event.

    He stood beside Xi at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen and smiled as Putin approached. Trump extended his hand and shook Putin’s as the Chinese leader looked on.

    Scott, a Trump ally in the Senate, said Tuesday he sees the president “trying to build relationships to try to make sure we don't end up at war [because] he doesn't like war.”.

    Trump signaled Monday that he might press Xi for details on an alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, costing the AI mogul his job as the organization’s president and CEO. He also said he could bring up Nvidia’s sales of sophisticated microchips that many lawmakers — Republican and Democrat — want to ensure remain in the U.S. for domestic AI development.

    The administration’s response to the turmoil at Nvidia, with Trump even suggesting he'd support Huang returning as CEO, is a rare area where Republicans have expressed concern publicly. House Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie, R-Kent., wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Wednesday seeking information about “the implementation of federal laws governing technology exports, in particular the application of export controls relating to semiconductor chips, the effect of which has a broad impact on America’s race with China to artificial intelligence (AI) dominance and the ability of U.S. companies to set global technology standards.”.

    Heather Williams, director of the Project on Nuclear Issues at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote this week that for the three leaders, the “path is fraught with challenges.”.

    “Putin could diplomatically outmaneuver the Trump administration and make any progress on nuclear complications dependent on undermining Western support to Ukraine,” she wrote in an analysis for the Washington, D.C.-based think tank. “Even the optics of Trump and Putin negotiating while the war continues and as Russia ramps up missile strikes on Ukrainian civilian targets could be interpreted as undermining U.S. values.”.

    • That hasn’t stopped her from often playing a key role in Trump’s agenda, casting a critical vote in Brett Kavanaugh’s confirmation to the Supreme Court.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Susan Collins, the five-term Republican from Maine, called her opponent Troy Jackson, a former logger and state senate president, to concede Tuesday night. The Associated Press called the election just after midnight, with Jackson leading by about six percentage points.

    Despite nearly 30 years in the Senate, Collins has been seen as one of the most vulnerable Republican incumbents, a smaller pebble in the blue avalanche that wiped out MAGA candidates in the midterm elections. She was the lone Senate Republican to represent a state that former Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris carried in the 2024 election. She lost despite her efforts to distance herself from President Donald Trump. Her campaign claims she has never voted for the president and reportedly refused his help with her run.

    That hasn’t stopped her from often playing a key role in Trump’s agenda, casting a critical vote in Brett Kavanaugh’s confirmation to the Supreme Court. Kavanaugh would later join the majority opinion in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, which overturned Roe v. Wade and ended the constitutional right to an abortion. Indeed, Collins’ position on reproductive rights seems to have played a key role in her defeat. Collins received support from Trump despite her efforts, according to reporting from ProPublica earlier this year, which revealed how an FBI anti-corruption squad was investigating Collins before Trump killed the case.

    As for Jackson, he first ran for office in 2000 as a Republican for the Maine House of Representatives, but lost. He ran again as an independent two years later and won, becoming the first non-Democrat to represent the area since the late ‘70s.

    Before delegates at a state convention chose Jackson in July, Collins was originally running against oyster farmer Graham Platner, who won the Democratic primary with support from progressive leaders. But controversies surrounding Platner continued to pile up, and he finally withdrew from the race on July 10 following sexual assault allegations.

    Fascism mixed into cringey online content is easy to mock – but no less dangerous

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This article was originally published on The Conversation.
    • In a recent development, against the backdrop of an unpopular war in Iran, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth confirmed on July 15, 2026, that the Pentagon would begin testing male service members 30 and older for low testosterone.
    • The combination of aggressive masculinity and militarism with the implications of testing for something like “spontaneous morning erections” as necessary for war fighting is emblematic of the administration’s tendency to combine fascist ideas and symbols with outright embarrassing messaging, or what I call “cringe fascism.”.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This article was originally published on The Conversation.

    In a recent development, against the backdrop of an unpopular war in Iran, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth confirmed on July 15, 2026, that the Pentagon would begin testing male service members 30 and older for low testosterone. That, the department later stated, would include assessing symptoms of low testosterone such as “reduced libido, loss of spontaneous morning erections, erectile dysfunction, diminished energy and physical performance, impaired concentration, reduced muscle mass, and depressed mood.”.

    The combination of aggressive masculinity and militarism with the implications of testing for something like “spontaneous morning erections” as necessary for war fighting is emblematic of the administration’s tendency to combine fascist ideas and symbols with outright embarrassing messaging, or what I call “cringe fascism.”.

    For some time there’s been a contentious debate among writers, historians and public intellectuals over whether Donald Trump’s presidency could be considered “fascist.” Some have argued that such claims are hyperbolic or inaccurate, while others say it is a useful and accurate ideological label.

    Either way, it would be difficult to deny that the Trump administration frequently draws from the well of fascist imagery and symbolism in its official messaging.

    And that’s where the concept of cringe fascism fits in. In online parlance,“cringe” is a kind of embarrassment by proxy when someone posts something that should be embarrassing but which doesn’t seem to be to them.

    For their part, members of the Trump administration have relied on language and symbolism that borrows from the fascist or authoritarian playbook while doing so in a way that commenters often mock as patently ridiculous or embarrassing – or cringe.

    Recent findings suggest that but the purported silliness of these ideas, as with Hegseth’s testosterone policy, hides a much more serious – and to some critics, fascist – reality. That, moreover, is why the deployment of cringe can be effective: It can generate enthusiasm among conservative voters by trolling the left while reducing deadly serious policy debates to the level of online memes.

    Industry observers note that as Americans prepare for the midterms and a surely contentious presidential election in 2028, such considerations of Trump’s authoritarian tendencies are being put to the test. That’s especially true as he consistently threatens the integrity of elections, deploys immigration and other federal law enforcement officers on American streets in a highly contested manner, and attempts to target the press and restrict its access.

    As a scholar of conspiracy theories, I have been amazed at some of the more blatant efforts to repurpose fascist imagery by members of Trump’s inner circle.

    It has been revealed that consider, for example, the use of ethnonationalist and fascist imagery of “blood and soil” in sloganeering by the Department of Homeland Security, or encouraging U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement recruits to “Defend the Homeland.”.

    Sources indicate that and then there are the attacks on the press as the “enemy of the people,” echoing past totalitarian leaders, followed by Trump’s banning of mainstream media from the White House and the launch of Trump TV as the state channel. Critics view such moves to attack and restrict the press as hallmarks of fascist methods.

    It has been revealed that borrowing more obviously from fascist tropes was Trump posting on social media a mock-up of a potential new Space Force uniform. The post claimed to draw inspiration from Paul Verhoeven’s “Starship Troopers,” in which the soldiers are deliberately modeled on the fascist aesthetic and ideology of the Nazis.

    Alongside the authoritarian and fascist tropes, the Trump administration cannot seem to avoid “cringe.”.

    Recent examples include the White House tweeting images of Trump as a videogame character on a select screen with sleeveless blue suit and bulging muscles, or sharing an AI parody of the new Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time game with an awkward video of a pixelated Trump running around the White House lawn. Or consider the post depicting Trump as Green Lantern, using his magic ring to raise a spectral border wall, launch a military attack and fix American industry.

    Sources indicate that on the one hand, the Trump administration seems determined to keep his party in power and enact a transformative MAGA policy agenda. On the other hand, Trump seems incapable of avoiding cringey riffs such as his digressions on men’s bodies in ways that seem strikingly at odds with his tough-guy persona. To see the commander in chief waxing poetic about Ohio Sen. Jon Husted’s rear feels deeply surreal.

    Trump’s seemingly incongruous comments occur at the same time that the secretary of defense is advocating hypermasculinity in the military through testosterone testing, reflecting a heady mix of masculinity and military supremacy that has long been a hallmark of fascism. Such a policy is also at odds with how the professional military has presented itself under previous administrations.

    The mixture of fascist aesthetics with cringe posting underscores the internal contradictions of the Trump administration.

    It is difficult to see critics’ view of Trump’s second term as “fascist” when observers get such awkward online displays of silliness. And when official communications from the White House and federal agencies are equal parts tough talk, trolling and cringe, the underlying policies can get lost in the shuffle.

    Sources indicate that is is hard to know whether this flood of cringe is always intentional, but it is certainly confusing and hilarious to both Trump’s supporters and his opponents. But that belies what many critics have decried as authoritarian actions by this administration, and these comparisons with fascism continue to animate public discourse.

    Masked ICE agents continue to operate with some legal protections from the White House in their sometimes-deadly efforts to pursue and round up people it broadly accuses of being in the country illegally.

    Likewise, the DHS announced that ICE agents could be deployed to polling locations, while the agency has reportedly attempted to get access to voter information to investigate alleged voter fraud through increased surveillance.

    The deployment of cringe might seems like a ridiculous, even unconscious, exercise by an administration that – as with the five-day tenure of former press secretary Katie Zacharia shows – regularly exposes itself to derision and satire. Yet that’s why the use of such a concept can be so strategically effective: It turns potentially deadly serious policy consequences and ideological choices into a game of memes and online gamesmanship.

    In a recent development, matthew N. Hannah, Associate Professor of Rhetoric, Politics and Culture, University of Wisconsin-Madison.

    It has been revealed that as we get closer to final results from the 2026 midterms, the scale of the carnage comes more clearly into view. The question is not whether Republicans can recover from this, but whether the American system of government will be changed irreparably before they do. To what will Republicans return?

    In the Senate, Democrats gained nine seats, the biggest swing since Republicans’ nine-seat pickup in 2014. With 56 senators, it’s the Democrats’ biggest majority since 2009–10, when they peaked at 60 seats. Republicans haven’t had that many Senate seats since 1922, when the caucus was 59 seats after the 1920 landslide that repudiated Woodrow Wilson’s progressivism and swept Warren Harding into office. If you’re wondering, the largest-ever Republican Senate caucus, in absolute numbers rather than as a share of the chamber, was 60 in 1907; the largest Democratic caucus was 75 seats at the peak of the Latest Deal in 1937. There’s a reason why Franklin D. Roosevelt thought he could get away with Court-packing with 75 senators.

    Dan McLaughlin is a senior writer at National Review Online and a fellow at National Review Institute.

    • The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.
    • Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.

    Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.

    The fate of the nominations and bills could ultimately be decided via a challenge on the Senate floor, according to a Democratic committee staffer, speaking on condition of anonymity.

    In a statement Wednesday morning, committee Democrats, led by ranking member  Maria Cantwell of Washington, mentioned they objected to Thumann Severs’ nomination without a Democratic “pair” nomination and referenced a letter they sent to Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, on Monday requesting the nomination be removed from the agenda.

    “Commissioner Anna Gomez could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times,” the group wrote. “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.”.

    Sources indicate that thumann Severs, if confirmed, would give the FCC three Republican members and one Democrat, Gomez. The three Republicans could then constitute a quorum on the commission, allowing President Donald Trump to potentially fire Gomez. The commission generally has five members, three of the president’s party and two in the minority.

    Cruz stated at the markup that there is nothing in the law that requires moving nominees in pairs, and that committee Republicans would continue their work on what he called a nomination that followed a “typical process.”.

    Sources indicate that “Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January,” Cruz noted. “But today is November 18th. The American people elected each of us to fulfill our duties, including advice and consent, for our full terms.”.

    Related: Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing.

    The Democratic staffer told reporters that because the committee did not adopt rules at the beginning of the 119th Congress, it has been operating under rules from the 118th, which required the attendance of at least one member of the minority party to constitute a quorum for reporting bills or nominations.

    In a recent development, “The remaining recourse is to basically go to the floor and . . . make an inquiry in terms of what took place today, and then there would have to be a formal ruling by the chair,” they remarked.

    They added that in determining whether the committee had a quorum to advance the nomination, “It would depend on how they view our committee rules from the 118th that we practice under for the 119th versus what the Senate rules are.” The staffer said they have not yet spoken with committee Democrats or Democratic leadership about plans for such an inquiry.

    It has been revealed that democrats also previously boycotted a committee markup in March over an aviation safety bill left off the committee’s agenda, after which action was deferred. The committee later came to agreement and rescheduled the markup.

    In their letter Monday, Democrats quoted Cruz from a 2014 statement about the nomination of Loretta Lynch to be attorney general.

    “As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the letter said.

    On Tuesday, Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., wrote his own letter to Cruz calling for the removal of the nomination from the agenda based on grounds that Thumann Severs lied to the committee.

    It has been revealed that “While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related concerns,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount,” Luján wrote.

    Democrats have criticized the FCC and Carr for allowing media consolidation, including by Skydance. There has also been bipartisan criticism of Carr’s threats against broadcasters for speech he disagrees with.

    Luján told reporters Wednesday prior to the markup that he expects, under Democratic control next year, Carr and potentially Thumann Severs would be called to testify.

    Industry observers note that “I have questions. I certainly hope that Brendan Carr will voluntarily show up to this committee when invited, and that other rules and tools do not need to be used,” Luján mentioned, responding to a question about possibly subpoenaing Carr. “But . . . everything should be on the table.”.

    According to recent reports, sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., said at the markup that he spoke with Thumann Severs about her role at the FCC and her “lack of engagement” as the commission has made decisions regarding broadcasters. He also said he found her testimony at last week’s nomination hearing “comforting.”.

    “I have concerns with FCC action in regard to political speech, broadcasters, and she indicated in her answers . . . in a way that provided me with a level of comfort about her nomination in regard to that matter,” Moran noted.

    Moran also stated he hopes to meet with Thumann Severs before her nomination is brought to the floor.
